wiki_content/macos-p1-finder-deep-dive.h.text:
macOS: P1: Finder Deep Dive
 Finder is the single app every other piece of Mac navigation eventually routes through. Most of what makes it fast is turned off by default or hidden behind a menu most people never open - this page turns all of it on. 
 The Sidebar
 Favorites
 - any folder you drag into this section for one-click access - your session folder, a scratch drive, anything you open constantly.
 Locations
 - This Mac, iCloud Drive, and any connected server all live here automatically.
 External drives
 - appear in the sidebar automatically the moment they are connected, with an eject icon next to each one.
 Four Ways to View a Folder
 Icon View
 - best for visually scanning thumbnails - picking out an image or a waveform preview by eye.
 List View
 - best for sorting by name, date, or size, and for scanning a long list of session files at once.
 Column View
 - best for drilling down through several nested folders quickly, since each click adds a column instead of replacing the window.
 Gallery View
 - a large preview pane plus a filmstrip - useful for previewing several files back to back without opening each one.
 Sorting, Grouping, and Searching
 Click any column header in List View to sort by it - clicking Date Modified twice puts the most recent files at the top. The View menu's Group By option clusters files by kind, date, or tag without changing the sort order underneath. The search field in the top right defaults to searching This Mac; a small scope bar lets you narrow it down to just the current folder instead. 
 [IMAGE: Finder View Options panel for a real folder, showing Group By, Sort By, icon size, text size]
 View Options (Command-J) for a specific folder - Group By, Sort By, and exactly which columns show up in List View, all set per-folder rather than globally. 
 Reading a Window Without Opening Anything
 Preview pane
 - turned on from View > Show Preview - shows a live preview of whatever is selected, alongside file details, without opening it.
 Status Bar
 - shows item count and free space at the bottom of the window.
 Path Bar
 - turned on from View > Show Path Bar - shows the exact nested-folder route to whatever is selected, as a row of clickable segments at the bottom of the window.
 [IMAGE: Required]
 Turn on the Path Bar and actually read it.
 The path bar is not decoration - it is the literal address of the selected item, one folder inside the next. Clicking any segment jumps straight to that folder. Enable View > Show Path Bar now and click through a few segments before moving on. 
 [IMAGE: A real Finder window with the Path Bar visible at the bottom, showing Macintosh HD > Library > Audio]
 The Path Bar in action at the bottom of a real Finder window - Macintosh HD, then Library, then Audio, each segment clickable. 
 Get Info and Finder Settings
 Command-I on any selected file opens Get Info - size, kind, exact location, tags, and a Sharing & Permissions section covered in depth on the Privacy and Security page. Finder's own preferences live under Finder > Settings, split into General, Tabs, Sidebar, and Advanced tabs. Advanced is where filename extensions and iCloud removal warnings are controlled, covered next on the File Extensions and File Types page. 
 Showing Hidden Files
 Shift-Command-. toggles whether hidden files and folders - anything starting with a dot, like .DS_Store - are visible in the current Finder window. These files exist for a reason and are hidden on purpose; toggling them visible for troubleshooting is fine, but nothing here should be deleted without knowing exactly what it does first. 
 Go to Folder
 Shift-Command-G opens a small text field where typing any path - ~/Music, /Library/Audio, or anything else - jumps directly there, instantly. This is dramatically faster than clicking through several nested folders by hand, and it is the standard way to reach folders, like the hidden user Library, that Finder does not show a shortcut to. 
 [IMAGE: The Go to Folder dialog with a real path typed in, showing autocomplete suggestions for nearby folders]
 Go to Folder, mid-type - notice the autocomplete offering nearby matching folders below the typed path, a fast way to catch a typo before pressing Return.

wiki_content/macos-p1-finder-smart-folde.title: macOS: P1: Finder Smart Folders
wiki_content/macos-p1-finder-smart-folde.text:
macOS: P1: Finder Smart Folders
 A Smart Folder looks like an ordinary folder in the sidebar, but it holds nothing at all. It is a saved search that runs live every time you open it, which makes it one of the more genuinely useful Finder features almost nobody turns on. 
 What a Smart Folder Actually Is
 A Smart Folder does not move, copy, or store a single file. It displays whatever currently matches a set of search criteria you define once, and that result list updates automatically every time you open it - a file that starts matching shows up without you doing anything, and a file that no longer matches disappears the same way. The files themselves never leave their real, original locations. 
 Building One
 The process is the same every time: 
 Open Finder. 
 Choose File > New Smart Folder. 
 Set the search scope to either This Mac or a specific location using the bar at the top of the window. 
 Click the + button to add a search criterion. 
 Combine as many criteria as needed - each additional + button adds another condition. 
 Click Save, give it a name, and choose whether to add it to the sidebar. 
 An Audio-Production Example
 A genuinely useful Smart Folder for this program: set the Kind criterion to Audio, add a second criterion for Date Modified within the last 7 days, and save it as "Recent Audio." The result is a folder that always shows whatever audio you have touched in the last week, across your entire Mac, without you ever having to remember where each file actually lives. 
 [IMAGE: Required]
 Build the Recent Audio Smart Folder and demonstrate it.
 Create the Smart Folder described above - Kind is Audio, Date Modified within the last 7 days - save it, and add it to the sidebar. Your screenshot for this step needs to show both the criteria you set and the resulting file list. 
 [IMAGE: Finder File menu with New Smart Folder highlighted]
 Starting the process: File > New Smart Folder. 
 [IMAGE: A saved Smart Folder icon, distinguished by its gear badge, named Perc Wav Files.savedSearch]
 A real saved Smart Folder - notice the gear icon on the folder, and the .savedSearch extension, marking it as a search rather than an ordinary folder. This one filters for percussion WAV files rather than the Recent Audio example above, but the mechanism is identical. 
 [IMAGE: An opened Smart Folder showing 345 live matching WAV file results]
 Opened, this Smart Folder shows 345 live results pulled from across the drive - none of these files were moved or duplicated to get here. 
 Why This Beats a Normal Folder
 A normal folder only contains what you manually drag into it, and it goes stale the moment a matching file gets added somewhere else or an old one gets deleted - nothing updates until you go fix it by hand. A Smart Folder never goes stale, because it is not really holding files at all; it is re-running its search every time it opens. The same file can also appear inside several different Smart Folders at once - a WAV file could show up in both a "Recent Audio" Smart Folder and a "Files Over 100 MB" Smart Folder simultaneously - without ever being duplicated on disk.

wiki_content/macos-p1-spotlight-quick-lo.title: macOS: P1: Spotlight, Quick Look, and Screenshots
wiki_content/macos-p1-spotlight-quick-lo.text:
macOS: P1: Spotlight, Quick Look, and Screenshots
 Three of the fastest tools on a Mac all skip a step other operating systems require. Spotlight skips navigating to an app. Quick Look skips opening one. The screenshot shortcuts skip a separate screenshot app entirely. 
 Spotlight: Search Everything at Once
 Command-Space opens Spotlight - a search box that finds apps, files, and even quick calculations by typing a few letters of a name, instead of navigating to them by hand. Type a few letters, watch the top result update live, and press Return to open it. This matters more than it sounds: instead of remembering that Audio MIDI Setup lives inside Applications > Utilities, typing "audio midi" into Spotlight and pressing Return gets there in about a second, every time, regardless of where the app actually lives on disk. 
 [IMAGE: Tip]
 Tip:
 Spotlight is almost always faster than digging through folders for anything you already know the name of. Save Finder navigation for when you are actually browsing, not searching.
 [IMAGE: Spotlight search for Audio MIDI Setup.app, showing it as the top result]
 Typing "audio MIDI Setup.app" into Spotlight brings it up as the top result instantly, no matter where the app actually lives on disk. 
 [IMAGE: Spotlight search for Pro Tools.app, showing it and several other related apps as results]
 Searching "Pro Tools.app" instead - Spotlight also surfaces close matches like Pro Tools First, useful when you are not sure of an app's exact name. 
 Quick Look: Preview Without Opening
 Select a file in Finder and press the Space bar. A preview window opens right there showing that file's actual content - an image, a PDF's pages, or a waveform for some audio formats - without launching the full app that normally handles it. Press Space again, or Escape, to close the preview. This is the fastest way to confirm a file is the one you want before committing to opening a heavier app around it. 
 [IMAGE: Quick Look preview of a selected WAV file, playing back with transport controls]
 Quick Look on a real WAV file, complete with playback controls - confirming this is the right vocal take without ever opening a full audio app. 
 Screenshots: Three Shortcuts to Know
 Shift-Command-3
 - captures the entire screen and saves it as a file, by default to the Desktop.
 Shift-Command-4
 - turns the pointer into a crosshair - click and drag to capture just a specific rectangular area of the screen.
 Shift-Command-5
 - opens a toolbar with every capture option in one place: whole screen, a window, a selected area, plus timed capture and a place to choose where files get saved.
 [IMAGE: The real Shift-Command-5 toolbar with its Options menu open, showing Save to, Timer, and Capture settings]
 The real toolbar, Options menu open - Save to, a capture Timer, Show Floating Thumbnail, Remember Last Selection, and Show Mouse Pointer all live here. 
 Screen Recording
 The same Shift-Command-5 toolbar also offers Record Entire Screen and Record Selected Portion. A still screenshot cannot show a stutter, a crash sequence, or a plugin misbehaving over time - a short screen recording can. When documenting a technical problem for an instructor or for tech support, a 15-second recording of the actual glitch happening is worth far more than a written description of it after the fact.

wiki_content/macos-p2-file-system-struct.title: macOS: P2: File-System Structure and Paths
wiki_content/macos-p2-file-system-struct.text:
macOS: P2: File-System Structure and Paths
 Every single thing on your Mac's drive lives at a specific, exact address. Learning that address system - where it starts, how it branches, and how to write it down - makes the rest of this unit, and a good chunk of Pro Tools troubleshooting, dramatically easier. 
 The Root of the Drive: /
 Every path on the Mac starts at exactly one place: the root, written as a single forward slash, /. Every folder on the drive, without exception, is either sitting directly inside root or nested inside another folder that eventually traces back to it. Four folders sit right at that root level and matter most for this unit - the same four shown in the screenshot at the top of this unit's first page. 
 /Applications
 - apps available to every account on the Mac.
 /Library
 - system-wide settings, support files, and plug-ins shared by every account - a different, visible folder from the hidden one inside your own user folder.
 /System
 - the operating system itself, on a read-only, signed volume since macOS Catalina.
 /Users
 - every account's home folder on this Mac lives here.
 Home: ~
 Your own personal folder, /Users/yourname, has a shortcut: the tilde, ~. Typing ~/Desktop means exactly the same thing as typing /Users/yourname/Desktop - the tilde always expands to your own home folder, whichever account is currently logged in. 
 ~/Desktop
 - files and folders visible on your Desktop.
 ~/Documents
 - the default save location for most documents.
 ~/Downloads
 - where browsers and Mail save downloaded files by default.
 ~/Music
 - the default location for Music.app's library and some audio apps' default save folder.
 ~/Library
 - hidden by default - your own personal settings and support files, covered in depth on its own page later in this unit.
 [IMAGE: Critical]
 /Library and ~/Library are genuinely different folders.
 They share a name, but they are not the same folder, not aliases of each other, and often hold completely different files for the very same piece of software - one copy shared by everyone, one copy scoped to just you. Confusing the two is the single most common file-system mistake in this entire unit. 
 What a Path Actually Is
 A path is the literal, unambiguous address of a file or folder - a chain of names separated by forward slashes, always starting from either root or home. An absolute path starts with / and spells out the entire route from root: /Users/yourname/Music/song.wav. The same file can be written starting from home instead: ~/Music/song.wav. Both point to the exact same file - they are just two different starting points for writing the same address. 
 Two tools from the Finder Deep Dive page work together here: the Path Bar reads a path back to you for whatever is selected, and Go to Folder lets you type a path in and jump straight there. Later in this unit, reaching your Pro Tools AAX plug-ins means typing /Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins directly into Go to Folder, rather than clicking through five nested windows by hand. 
 [IMAGE: Required]
 Screenshot both the root level and your own Home folder.
 Show a Finder window at the very root of the drive with Library, System, Users, and Applications visible, and a second screenshot of your own Home folder showing Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Music, and Library. 
 [ Screenshot still needed - a Finder window at the root of the drive showing Library, System, Users, and Applications ]
 [IMAGE: A real Home folder listing at /Users/adamwolson, showing Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Dropbox, Library]
 A real Home folder - Desktop, Documents, Downloads, and the rest sit alongside whatever personal folders someone has added over time, all still inside that same one account folder.

wiki_content/macos-p2-file-extensions-an.title: macOS: P2: File Extensions and File Types
wiki_content/macos-p2-file-extensions-an.text:
macOS: P2: File Extensions and File Types
 The letters after the last dot in a filename are not decoration. They are a label telling macOS, and every app on it, exactly how to interpret the data stored inside that file - and macOS hides that label by default. 
 What an Extension Actually Tells You
 An extension is a short suffix - .wav, .zip, .app - that identifies a file's format. Double-clicking a file makes macOS look at its extension to decide which app should open it. The extension is metadata about the file, not the content of the file itself; changing it does not touch a single byte of the actual data inside. 
 Extensions You'll See Constantly in This Program
 .ptx
 - a Pro Tools session file - the project itself, not the audio inside it.
 .wav / .aif / .aiff
 - uncompressed audio - the standard formats for tracking and mixing.
 .mp3
 - compressed, lossy audio - fine for reference, not for production work.
 .mov / .mp4
 - video containers, common for picture-sync work and screen recordings.
 .zip
 - a compressed archive, covered in depth on the Copying, Moving, and Archiving Files page.
 .dmg / .pkg / .app
 - Mac disk images, installer packages, and application bundles, covered in depth on the Installing Software page.
 .aaxplugin
 - Avid's plug-in format for Pro Tools - a package, not a single file, covered on the Library vs. System page.
 Turning Extensions On
 macOS hides most extensions by default, showing a clean file name instead. Turn this off from Finder > Settings > Advanced, and check Show all filename extensions. With it on, every file in every Finder window shows its true format at a glance - essential for confirming you are about to submit a PDF and not an accidentally-saved .docx. 
 [IMAGE: Required]
 Enable extensions and confirm it.
 Turn on Show all filename extensions in Finder > Settings > Advanced, then open a folder containing a mix of file types and confirm each one now shows its extension. 
 [IMAGE: Finder Settings Advanced tab with Show all filename extensions checked]
 Show all filename extensions, checked - along with the other Advanced settings covered on the Finder Deep Dive page, like the warning before changing an extension and the search scope default. 
 Changing an Extension Doesn't Change the File
 Renaming song.wav to song.mp3 does not compress or re-encode a single sample of audio. The file's actual content - the raw audio data inside - is completely untouched; only the label changed. What usually happens next is that whichever app tries to open it gets confused, because the label now promises a format the data does not actually match, and the file either fails to open or opens as garbled noise. The only way to actually convert a file's format is to export or bounce it through an app that reads the original format and writes a new file in the target format - renaming is never a substitute for conversion.

wiki_content/macos-p2-files-folders-appl.title: macOS: P2: Files, Folders, Applications, Packages, and Aliases
wiki_content/macos-p2-files-folders-appl.text:
macOS: P2: Files, Folders, Applications, Packages, and Aliases
 Finder shows several different kinds of things that all look similar at a glance - an icon and a name - but behave in genuinely different ways underneath. Telling them apart correctly prevents a lot of confusion later in this unit. 
 Six Things That Can Sit in a Finder Window
 File
 - a single unit of data - a document, an audio file, an image.
 Folder
 - a container that holds files and other folders, with no content of its own.
 Application
 - a program you run, most often appearing as a single icon even though it is really a package underneath - see below.
 Package (or bundle)
 - a folder disguised, on purpose, as a single file. Every application on the Mac is actually a package holding its real code and resources inside.
 Alias
 - a pointer to another file or folder somewhere else, marked with a small arrow badge on its icon. It takes almost no space and does not duplicate anything.
 Disk image / installer package
 - a .dmg mounts as a virtual disk, and a .pkg runs a scripted install - both covered in full on the Installing Software page.
 Looking Inside a Package
 Control-click any application and choose Show Package Contents. Finder opens the package as an ordinary folder, revealing a Contents folder inside holding pieces like MacOS (the actual program code), Resources (icons, sounds, images the app uses), and Info.plist (a small file describing the app to macOS). This is exactly how a single application icon can actually contain hundreds of internal files while still behaving like one double-clickable item. 
 [IMAGE: Warning]
 Look, do not touch.
 Opening a package's contents to understand how it is built is completely safe. Moving, renaming, or deleting anything inside it is not - a package with a missing internal file usually stops working entirely, sometimes without a clear error message explaining why. 
 [IMAGE: Right-click context menu on Google Slides.app with Show Package Contents highlighted]
 Control-click on a real app - Show Package Contents sits right below Open. 
 [IMAGE: The resulting Contents folder for Google Slides.app, showing Resources, MacOS, _CodeSignature, Info.plist]
 Inside: Resources, MacOS (the actual program code), _CodeSignature, Info.plist, and CodeResources - exactly the internal structure described above, on a real installed app. 
 Aliases vs. the Real File
 An alias looks almost identical to the file it points to, but a small arrow badge in the corner of its icon gives it away. Double-clicking an alias opens the original file, wherever that original actually lives - the alias itself holds no real content. Deleting an alias does nothing to the original file. Deleting or moving the original, however, breaks every alias pointing at it, leaving each one pointing at nothing until it is either fixed or removed. 
 [IMAGE: A folder alias icon, distinguished by its small arrow badge, named CD alias]
 A real alias - the small arrow badge in the bottom-left corner is the only visual difference from the original folder it points to.

wiki_content/macos-p2-copying-moving-and.title: macOS: P2: Copying, Moving, and Archiving Files
wiki_content/macos-p2-copying-moving-and.text:
macOS: P2: Copying, Moving, and Archiving Files
 Dragging a file feels like the simplest thing you can do on a Mac, but what actually happens - a copy or a move - quietly depends on where you drag it, and getting that wrong is one of the most common causes of a Pro Tools session that suddenly can't find its own audio. 
 Same Drive vs. Different Drive
 Dragging a file within the same drive moves it - the file leaves its original folder entirely and exists only in the new location. Dragging a file to a different drive copies it instead - the original stays exactly where it was, and a second, independent copy appears in the new location. Same gesture, two different outcomes, decided entirely by whether the destination is on the same physical drive. 
 Forcing the Opposite with Option
 Holding Option while dragging within the same drive forces a copy instead of a move, leaving the original untouched. There is rarely a need to force a move across drives, since that is already the default there - Option-drag matters almost exclusively for same-drive copying. 
 Duplicating and Aliases
 Command-D
 - duplicates the selected item in place, appending "copy" to its name.
 Alias
 - a lightweight pointer to the original file, covered in full on the Files, Folders, Applications, Packages, and Aliases page - not the same thing as a duplicate.
 The Trash: Deleting, Restoring, Emptying
 Moving a file to the Trash does not delete it - it relocates the file into a holding folder, still fully recoverable. Right-click any item in the Trash and choose Put Back to restore it to its original location. Nothing is actually deleted, and no space is reclaimed, until you choose Empty Trash, which asks for confirmation before permanently removing everything inside. 
 [IMAGE: Critical]
 Moving session audio outside its expected location breaks the session.
 Pro Tools sessions reference their audio files by location. Moving, renaming, or relocating a source WAV file outside the Audio Files folder Pro Tools expects it in produces a missing-file warning the next time that session opens, forcing a manual relink before playback works again. When in doubt, leave session media exactly where it was recorded or imported. 
 ZIP Archives
 Right-click any file or folder and choose Compress to create a .zip archive - a single file containing a compressed copy of everything selected. The original folder is untouched; the .zip is an entirely separate file sitting alongside it. Double-clicking a .zip extracts its contents into a new folder, decompressed and ready to use, again without touching the .zip file itself. Always open the extracted folder and confirm every expected file is present and plays back correctly before deleting either the original folder or the .zip - a corrupted archive fails silently far more often than it fails loudly. 
 [IMAGE: Right-click context menu on a folder with Compress highlighted]
 The right-click context menu with Compress selected - macOS names the resulting .zip after the folder automatically, leaving the original folder completely untouched alongside it. 
 [IMAGE: The resulting .zip file icon, sitting at 3.1 MB, from the Compress action]
 The finished archive - a completely separate file from the original folder, with its own size on disk.

wiki_content/macos-p3-installing-softwar.title: macOS: P3: Installing Software - DMG, APP, and PKG
wiki_content/macos-p3-installing-softwar.text:
macOS: P3: Installing Software - DMG, APP, and PKG
 Getting software onto a Mac almost always means working with three things: a DMG that delivers it, an APP that you actually run, and sometimes a PKG that installs it into places a simple drag cannot reach. Windows software works differently enough that treating an EXE as a Mac equivalent causes more confusion than it resolves. 
 What a DMG Actually Is
 A DMG is a disk image. Double-clicking one mounts a virtual disk on your desktop and in the Finder sidebar, exactly like inserting a physical disk. Most DMGs contain nothing but the app itself and a shortcut arrow pointing at the Applications folder. "Installing" the app means dragging it onto that arrow - there is no installer program running, no script executing, and no separate uninstall step beyond dragging the app to the Trash later. A DMG is a delivery container, not itself the final installed location of anything - once you have dragged the app out of it, the mounted DMG can be ejected and the downloaded .dmg file thrown away. 
 The App Store
 The Mac App Store skips DMGs and PKGs entirely. Clicking Get or Install downloads and places the app directly into your Applications folder, keeps it updated automatically, and ties its license to your Apple Account rather than a serial number you have to track yourself. Not every piece of software this program uses is available there - Pro Tools and most professional audio software are not - but for everyday utilities it is often the simplest path. 
 Where EXE Fits In
 An EXE is a Windows executable format - not a Mac installer choice at all, and not a direct equivalent to anything covered on this page. macOS cannot run an EXE under any circumstances; it is built for an entirely different operating system, not just a different container format. If you ever see a .exe file, it is Windows-only software, full stop. 
 [IMAGE: Note]
 Three Mac concepts, not two Mac-vs-Windows ones.
 DMG, APP, and PKG are the three things to actually know on a Mac. A DMG is just a container for delivering files. An APP is the program itself. A PKG is an installer program that actively does something - the closest match to a Windows EXE, covered next. 
 When a Mac App Needs More Than a Drag
 Some software has to place files in protected system locations that a simple drag-and-drop cannot reach - audio interface drivers, Audio Unit plug-ins inside /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins, or components that need to register with the operating system. For that, Mac software uses a .pkg installer, built with Apple's Installer.app format. 
 .pkg installer
 - runs a scripted install, can write to system-level folders, and asks for your admin password - the closest functional match to a Windows EXE. A .pkg is frequently bundled inside a DMG alongside, or instead of, a plain .app.
 [IMAGE: Flow diagram comparing a Mac DMG and pkg installer path against a Windows EXE installer path]
 Diagram: how a DMG, a .pkg, and a Windows EXE each end up putting files on the system. 
 [IMAGE: Critical]
 Only download installers from the developer's own site.
 A Gatekeeper warning that a file "cannot be opened because it is from an unidentified developer" exists to protect you from exactly this. Never bypass that warning for software from a source you have not verified. 
 Real-World Examples
 Not every DMG looks the same. These four are all real installers, and each does something slightly different. 
 [IMAGE: Skim DMG window showing the app icon, an arrow, and the Applications folder icon with the instruction to drag one]
 Skim: the classic pattern. Drag the app icon onto the Applications shortcut and the install is finished. 
 [IMAGE: Dropbox installer DMG window with a single app icon and the instruction to double-click it]
 Dropbox: instead of dragging, you double-click the icon directly, which runs a short first-time setup before placing the app. 
 [IMAGE: Apogee Control 2 installer DMG showing a separate Software Installer pkg and a Software Uninstaller app]
 Apogee Control 2: a .pkg installer for the driver, plus something rare on a Mac - a dedicated uninstaller app, included specifically because a driver-level install needs a clean way back out. 
 [IMAGE: AIR Effects Bundle DMG containing only a single pkg installer, with no app to drag]
 AIR Effects Bundle: nothing to drag at all - just a .pkg. Double-clicking it runs the scripted install directly.

wiki_content/macos-p3-removing-applicati.title: macOS: P3: Removing Applications and Leftovers
wiki_content/macos-p3-removing-applicati.text:
macOS: P3: Removing Applications and Leftovers
 Most Mac software installs itself with a single drag, and uninstalls with a single delete - but that simplicity hides a few files that get left behind every time. Knowing where those files go, and when to use something more thorough than the Trash, keeps a Mac clean over years of installing and removing audio software. 
 Why Most Mac Apps Don't Need an Installer
 A typical Mac app is a single, self-contained .app bundle - all of its code and resources live inside that one bundle. Copying it into the Applications folder is the entire installation. There is no separate install program to run, and no registry to write to, because there is no registry on macOS at all. 
 What Actually Happens When You Delete an App
 Dragging an app to the Trash removes only the .app bundle itself. It does not remove any of the following: 
 Applications
 - the .app bundle itself - the only thing a simple Trash drag actually removes.
 ~/Library/Preferences
 - the app's saved settings file, one small .plist per app.
 ~/Library/Application Support
 - presets, templates, caches, and license or activation data - scoped to your account.
 /Library/Application Support
 - the same kind of data, but shared system-wide across every account.
 Plug-in locations
 - Audio Unit, VST, and AAX plug-ins the app installed, which do not live inside the app itself and are never touched by deleting it.
 LaunchAgents and LaunchDaemons
 - background helpers the app installed to run automatically, covered in full on the Login Items, Launch Agents, and Launch Daemons page.
 Over months or years, these leftover files accumulate across every app that was ever tried and later deleted - quietly consuming space, and occasionally causing conflicts if the same app is reinstalled later and finds its old settings still sitting there. 
 When to Use a Manufacturer's Uninstaller Instead
 Professional audio software that installs drivers, kernel-level components, or Launch Daemons often ships its own dedicated uninstaller app precisely because a simple Trash drag cannot cleanly reverse that kind of install. Apogee's Control 2 installer, covered on the Installing Software page, is a real example - it includes a Software Uninstaller app alongside its installer specifically so a driver-level install has a clean, complete way back out. When an uninstaller is provided, use it instead of dragging the app to the Trash. 
 Why Apps Like Hazel Exist
 Hazel, and similar utilities such as AppCleaner, watch for the moment you drag an app to the Trash and automatically search the common Library locations for that same app's leftover files, offering to remove everything at once. 
 [IMAGE: Note]
 This is not a Windows-style uninstaller.
 Hazel is not running an uninstall script the way Windows' Add or Remove Programs does - there is no registry to clean on a Mac. It is specifically hunting down the scattered Library files that a simple drag-to-Trash leaves behind, and it is a different tool from a manufacturer's dedicated uninstaller. 
 [IMAGE: Diagram showing an app being dragged to the Trash while its preferences file and Application Support folder remain]
 Diagram: what a simple drag-to-Trash actually removes, and what it leaves behind. 
 [IMAGE: Required]
 Find a real leftover folder.
 Locate a folder inside ~/Library/Preferences or ~/Library/Application Support belonging to an app that no longer appears in your Applications folder, and screenshot it. 
 [IMAGE: A real leftover folder in Application Support named TurboTax 2023, holding Forms, licensing files]
 A real example - TurboTax 2023, sitting in Application Support with Forms, licensing files, and settings intact, long after tax season and likely long after the app itself was deleted.

wiki_content/macos-p3-login-items-launch.title: macOS: P3: Login Items, Launch Agents, and Launch Daemons
wiki_content/macos-p3-login-items-launch.text:
macOS: P3: Login Items, Launch Agents, and Launch Daemons
 Some apps start themselves the moment you log in, and some run in the background permanently without ever opening a window at all. Both behaviors are controlled by the same underlying system, visible at two different levels - one you manage yourself, and one macOS manages for every app that asks. 
 Login Items and Background Items
 System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions lists every app set to open automatically when you log in, plus every background item currently running that did not need you to open anything at all. The "Open at Login" list is one you edit directly - add an app you want to start automatically, or remove one you are tired of seeing launch every morning. The background items list below it is different: it shows helper processes and extensions that other apps installed and manage themselves, which is exactly why an audio interface's control panel, or a plug-in license manager, can be running even when you have never manually opened it and its main app is not on screen. 
 [IMAGE: Note]
 Login Items are the visible surface of a bigger system.
 Everything listed under background items in Login Items & Extensions is, underneath, either a Launch Agent or a Launch Daemon - the two mechanisms covered for the rest of this page. Login Items & Extensions is the friendly front door; Launch Agents and Launch Daemons are the actual machinery behind it. 
 [IMAGE: System Settings General Login Items and Extensions panel]
 A real Login Items & Extensions panel - the Open at Login list above, and App Background Activity toggles below, each one a background item running on its own. 
 What launchd Actually Does
 launchd is the first process macOS starts at boot, and it never quits. Every other background process on the Mac - system service or third-party helper - is started, supervised, and eventually stopped by launchd, based on the instructions written inside a .plist configuration file. 
 Launch Agents
 A Launch Agent runs inside a logged-in user's session. It can draw a window, show a menu bar icon, or ask for input, because it has access to that user's full desktop environment. Agents start after login, and if two accounts are logged in on the same Mac, each gets its own separate copy of the same agent. 
 ~/Library/LaunchAgents
 - agents that belong to your user account only.
 /Library/LaunchAgents
 - agents installed for every account on the Mac, though each still runs separately per logged-in user rather than as one shared process.
 /System/Library/LaunchAgents
 - Apple's own agents, protected by System Integrity Protection.
 Launch Daemons
 A Launch Daemon runs as root, with no user session and no ability to show a window. Daemons start at boot, before anyone logs in, and keep running even if every user logs out. There is no per-user LaunchDaemons folder - a daemon is system-wide by definition. 
 /Library/LaunchDaemons
 - third-party daemons - most audio interface drivers install one here.
 /System/Library/LaunchDaemons
 - Apple's own system services, protected by System Integrity Protection.
 [IMAGE: Note]
 The short version:
 An Agent runs as you, can show UI, and starts at login. A Daemon runs as root, shows nothing, and starts at boot.
 [IMAGE: Side-by-side comparison diagram of Launch Agent versus Launch Daemon properties]
 Diagram: Launch Agent vs. Launch Daemon, compared by who runs them, whether they can show UI, when they start, and where their files live. 
 [IMAGE: Three real Finder windows side by side showing the contents of Library LaunchAgents, Library LaunchDaemons]
 All three folders, for real, side by side - /Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchDaemons, and ~/Library/LaunchAgents - each holding dozens of real .plist files from software installed over time. Notice the matching "- Archive" folders below them, where macOS moves old entries during major updates rather than deleting them outright. 
 Who Installs These, and Why
 Audio interface driver installers (Focusrite, Universal Audio, RME, and similar), the iLok License Manager, and Adobe and Microsoft update helpers all drop a Launch Agent or Launch Daemon during installation. That is how they keep running quietly in the background instead of requiring you to open them by hand every time you turn the Mac on. 
 [IMAGE: Warning]
 Watch for this in troubleshooting.
 A stuck or corrupted Launch Agent is one of the most common reasons a plug-in or audio interface refuses to authorize, or a Mac feels slow immediately after login. 
 Inspecting and Managing Them
 launchctl list
 - run in Terminal, prints every Launch Agent currently loaded for your user account.
 Activity Monitor
 - shows every running process, agent or daemon, under the Process Name column, with its parent process visible.
 launchctl bootout
 - unloads a specific Launch Agent or Daemon by its .plist path, stopping it until the Mac restarts or it is reloaded.
 [IMAGE: Terminal window showing the output of launchctl list, a long column of PIDs, statuses, and Agent labels]
 A real launchctl list output. Recognizable entries like com.noodlesoft.HazelHelper and com.audinate.dante.DanteVia.DanteViaLoader show exactly the kind of third-party Agent covered above. 
 [IMAGE: Note]
 This only shows Agents, not Daemons.
 A plain launchctl list run as yourself lists Agents running in your own session. Root-level Daemons do not show up here - seeing those requires running sudo launchctl list instead. 
 [IMAGE: Tip]
 Tip:
 Do not remove a Launch Agent or Daemon you do not recognize without researching the name first. Some are essential to macOS itself, and Apple's own agents in /System are protected from casual deletion anyway.

wiki_content/macos-p3-terminal-basics.ht.title: macOS: P3: Terminal Basics
wiki_content/macos-p3-terminal-basics.ht.text:
macOS: P3: Terminal Basics
 Terminal is a text-based way to talk directly to macOS, typing commands instead of clicking icons. A handful of commands turn it from an intimidating black box into a genuinely useful tool for an audio engineer - one that can tell you more about a WAV file in five seconds than digging through an app's Get Info window ever could. 
 Where Terminal Lives
 Terminal.app sits inside Applications > Utilities, alongside Console, Disk Utility, and Audio MIDI Setup - the folder Apple reserves for the built-in tools that manage the Mac itself. Opening it drops you at a prompt showing your username, your Mac's name, and a blinking cursor waiting for a command. 
 Terminal Commands Worth Trying
 Each of these does something real and immediately visible - copy any of them in, try it, and see what happens. 
 open .
 - opens the current Terminal location as a real Finder window - the fastest bridge back from the command line to the graphical interface, and proof that a period on its own means "right here."
 afinfo
 - prints the technical details of an audio file - sample rate, channel count, duration, bit depth, and format. Type afinfo followed by a space, then drag a WAV or AIFF file from Finder into the Terminal window and press Return.
 afplay
 - plays an audio file straight through the Mac's speakers, no app required. Type afplay followed by a space, drag in an audio file, and press Return.
 system_profiler SPAudioDataType
 - lists every audio device macOS currently recognizes. If an interface is missing from a DAW, this checks whether macOS itself can even see it - a real troubleshooting step, not just a demo.
 caffeinate
 - keeps the Mac from sleeping for as long as it runs - useful during a long file transfer or bounce. Press Control-C to stop it.
 [IMAGE: Tip]
 Start with afinfo.
 This is the command that makes the whole page click. Drag one of your own session's WAV files into a Terminal window after typing afinfo, and macOS hands back its exact sample rate, channel count, and format - proof that the operating system itself understands audio, underneath whatever DAW happens to be running. 
 Drag Files Into Terminal
 This is probably the single most useful trick on this page. Typing out a full file path by hand is slow and easy to get wrong - instead, start typing a command, add a space, and drag the file itself from Finder directly into the Terminal window. macOS inserts the complete, correct path automatically, spaces and all. 
 Type afinfo, add a space, then drag in a file named My Mix.wav. Terminal fills in something like afinfo /Users/yourname/Desktop/My\ Mix.wav on its own - notice the backslash before the space, which is just how Terminal marks a space that is part of a filename rather than a break between words. There is no need to type any of that by hand; dragging the file does it correctly every time. 
 Just Enough Navigation
 ls
 - list - shows every file and folder inside the current directory.
 cd
 - change directory - moves into a different folder, typed as cd followed by a path.
 open .
 - opens the current folder in Finder - already covered above, and worth knowing as a navigation command too.
 [IMAGE: Terminal window showing pwd, ls, and cd Documents run in sequence with real output after each command]
 ls listing a folder's contents, and cd Documents moving into a subfolder - the prompt itself updates to show the new location. 
 Tab Completion
 Start typing a file or folder name and press Tab. Terminal completes the name automatically when it can, or shows every match if more than one name fits. This saves typing and helps prevent path errors. 
 [IMAGE: Critical]
 Do not paste Terminal commands from the internet unless you understand what they do.
 Terminal commands can make system-level changes very quickly. Be especially cautious with anything containing sudo, which gives a command full administrator privileges. The commands on this page are safe to experiment with - but do not assume every command found online carries the same low risk.

wiki_content/macos-p3-privacy-and-securi.title: macOS: P3: Privacy and Security
wiki_content/macos-p3-privacy-and-securi.text:
macOS: P3: Privacy and Security
 Every piece of hardware and software that needs deep access to your Mac - a microphone, a camera, an audio interface driver - has to get your explicit permission first. This page covers where that permission lives and how driver installation actually works underneath it. 
 The Privacy and Security Pane
 Open System Settings > Privacy & Security. This pane gates which apps can access sensitive hardware and data: Microphone, Camera, Screen Recording, Full Disk Access, Accessibility, and Files and Folders each get their own list of allowed apps. 
 Microphone
 - required by Pro Tools and many audio interfaces for input monitoring. If input monitoring silently fails, check whether access was ever denied here.
 Accessibility
 - required by some control surface software and MIDI utilities that need to observe or control other apps on the Mac.
 Full Disk Access
 - required by some backup and file-management utilities to read protected system locations.
 [IMAGE: Note]
 A silent denial looks identical to a bug.
 If Pro Tools or a plug-in never even asks for a permission and simply does not work, the most likely explanation is that permission was denied once, in the past, and macOS is not asking again. 
 Gatekeeper
 Gatekeeper is the layer that warns you when opening software from a developer Apple has not verified. The warning reads that the app cannot be opened because it is from an unidentified developer. After that first block, the same app can be allowed manually from the Security section of Privacy & Security. 
 Installing Drivers: Kernel Extensions vs. System Extensions
 Audio interface drivers used to install as Kernel Extensions, or kexts - code running with full access to the operating system's core, the kernel. That access is powerful, but a faulty kext can crash the entire Mac, not just one app. 
 Modern macOS pushes hardware vendors toward System Extensions instead. A System Extension provides similar functionality without full kernel-level access, running in a more contained, safer space. 
 [IMAGE: Illustrative diagram of a Privacy and Security pane]
 Illustrative diagram, not an exact screenshot of macOS - shows the layout of a permission list and a blocked driver awaiting approval. 
 Approving a Newly Installed Driver
 macOS blocks a newly installed driver until it is approved manually. The typical sequence is install, restart, open Privacy & Security, click Allow next to the blocked extension, then restart again. 
 [IMAGE: Warning]
 Skipping approval is the most common cause of a driver that installs but does nothing.
 A brand-new audio interface driver can install successfully and still leave the interface invisible to Pro Tools if the approval step in Privacy & Security was never completed. 
 Privacy Permissions vs. File-System Permissions
 The word "permissions" means two unrelated things on a Mac, and mixing them up leads to looking in the wrong place entirely. Privacy permissions - Microphone, Camera, Accessibility, Full Disk Access, Files and Folders - control which apps are allowed to access specific hardware or protected data, and they live in Privacy & Security, covered above. 
 File-system permissions are a completely different concept: they control who can read, write, or execute a specific file or folder, and they live in Finder, under Get Info > Sharing & Permissions. Every file and folder has an owner, a group, and an "everyone" setting, each with its own Read, Write, or No Access level. A permissions problem here looks different from a privacy problem - instead of an app asking for access, you get an error trying to save, move, or delete a file because your account does not have Write access to it. 
 [IMAGE: Get Info window for a real WAV file, expanded to show Sharing and Permissions with owner, group]
 Get Info on a real audio file, with Sharing & Permissions expanded - the owner has Read & Write, the admin group has Read & Write, and everyone else has Read only.

wiki_content/macos-p4-system-diagnostic-.title: macOS: P4: System Diagnostic Tools
wiki_content/macos-p4-system-diagnostic-.text:
macOS: P4: System Diagnostic Tools
 Three built-in apps answer three different questions about your Mac: what hardware is actually connected, what is using resources right now, and what has the system been logging in the background. Learning all three turns troubleshooting from guesswork into a process. 
 System Information
 Open it from the Apple menu > About This Mac > More Info > System Report, or search for it directly in Spotlight. The sidebar organizes every category of hardware and software on the Mac - Hardware (CPU, Memory, Storage, USB, Thunderbolt/USB4, Audio, Bluetooth, and more), Network, and Software. 
 [IMAGE: System Information window showing the USB category with a tree of connected USB hubs and devices]
 The USB category, expanded to show every hub and device in the chain, along with each device's connection type and link speed. 
 This view lists every connected USB device in a tree, including hubs, along with the link speed each one is negotiating - 5 Gb/s or 10 Gb/s, for example. This is the first place to check when Pro Tools does not see an interface: if the device is missing here entirely, the problem is a cable, a port, or power - not Pro Tools. 
 [IMAGE: Note]
 Windows equivalent.
 Windows' closest match to this hardware tree is Device Manager. The Windows "System Information" app (run via msinfo32) is closer to a general system summary than to the detailed hardware tree shown here. 
 Activity Monitor
 Open it from Applications > Utilities > Activity Monitor. Five tabs - CPU, Memory, Energy, Disk, and Network - each sort every running process by that specific resource. 
 [IMAGE: Activity Monitor CPU tab showing running processes sorted by percent CPU usage]
 The CPU tab, sorted by % CPU, with the system-wide load summary at the bottom. 
 % CPU / CPU Time
 - how much processing power a process is using right now, and its running total since it launched.
 Threads / Idle Wake Ups
 - how many parallel execution paths a process is using, and how often it wakes the CPU from an idle state - a high wake count can point to a background app draining resources unnecessarily.
 PID / User
 - the process's unique ID number, and which account owns it.
 Real Mem / Private Mem
 - how much RAM the process is actually using right now, versus memory only that process can access.
 When Pro Tools' meters spike or an interface glitches, sort the CPU tab by % CPU to find whichever background process is stealing processing power. The summary bar at the bottom - System, User, and Idle percentages, plus total Threads and Processes - shows at a glance whether the whole Mac is under real load or one runaway app is the culprit. 
 The Other Four Tabs
 Memory
 - shows a Memory Pressure graph at the bottom: green means plenty of headroom, yellow means macOS is starting to work harder to manage memory, and red means it is actively struggling and swapping to disk - the exact moment a session starts to stutter.
 Energy
 - ranks processes by power impact, most useful for tracking down what is draining a laptop battery fast.
 Disk
 - shows read and write activity per process, useful when session playback stutters and RAM is not the bottleneck - the drive itself might be.
 Network
 - shows data sent and received per process, useful for catching a cloud-sync app or an auto-updater competing for bandwidth or system resources mid-session.
 [IMAGE: Note]
 Applications vs. background processes.
 Activity Monitor lists both at once, with no visual separator by default. An application is something you opened yourself and see in the Dock; a background process is everything else - system services, Launch Agents, helper apps - running without ever appearing as a window. A process consuming heavy CPU without a Dock icon to match is almost always a background item worth investigating, not a bug in Activity Monitor. 
 Console
 Open it from Applications > Utilities > Console. Console reads the system log - every message macOS and its apps write about what they are doing, including errors and crash reports. 
 [IMAGE: Console app open with no messages showing, before streaming has started]
 Console before pressing Start streaming. The sidebar lists connected Devices, and Reports for Crash, Spin, Log, and Diagnostic reports. 
 Devices
 - the Mac itself, plus any connected iOS devices, each with its own log stream.
 Reports
 - Crash Reports, Spin Reports, Log Reports, and Diagnostic Reports - saved records rather than a live stream.
 [IMAGE: Warning]
 Streaming live logs affects performance.
 Console warns that streaming log messages will impact system performance. Turn streaming on only while actively troubleshooting a specific problem, not as a background habit. 
 After a Pro Tools crash, Console's Crash Reports section under Reports holds a detailed log of exactly what failed - the single most useful place to look before contacting support. 
 [IMAGE: Required]
 Work from hardware down to software.
 Check System Information first to confirm a device physically exists and is recognized. Check Activity Monitor next to see what is actually running. Check Console last to read what the system logged about it. That order narrows a problem fastest.

wiki_content/macos-p4-force-quit-and-tro.title: macOS: P4: Force Quit and Troubleshooting
wiki_content/macos-p4-force-quit-and-tro.text:
macOS: P4: Force Quit and Troubleshooting
 A frozen app is not a reason to hold down the power button. macOS has a graduated set of tools for exactly this situation, each one more forceful than the last, and working through them in order solves almost everything without ever risking an unclean shutdown. 
 Getting There Fast: Option-Command-Escape
 Option-Command-Escape opens the Force Quit Applications window immediately, skipping the Apple menu entirely. It lists every running app; selecting one and clicking Force Quit ends it right away, without waiting for that app to finish whatever it was doing. 
 [IMAGE: Force Quit Applications window listing running apps, with one selected and the Force Quit button available]
 The Force Quit Applications window - select an app from the list and click Force Quit. Note the reminder at the bottom: this exact window opens with Option-Command-Escape. 
 Five Levels, From Gentlest to Last Resort
 Quit (Command-Q)
 - asks the app to close itself normally, saving anything it needs to first. This only works if the app is still responding.
 Force Quit (Option-Command-Escape)
 - ends an unresponsive app immediately, with no chance to save unsaved work in that app - use this once Quit has failed to do anything for a few seconds.
 Activity Monitor Quit
 - select the process in Activity Monitor, click the X button, and choose Quit - functionally the same gentle request as Command-Q, just reachable when the app itself is too frozen to show a Quit menu.
 Activity Monitor Force Quit
 - the same button's more forceful option - ends the process immediately, useful when a background process with no visible window or Dock icon needs to be stopped.
 Restart the Mac
 - the last resort, reserved for when the whole system - not just one app - has stopped responding to any of the above.
 A Sensible Order to Actually Follow
 Try Command-Q first and give it a few seconds - many apparent freezes are just a slow save or a large file operation finishing. If nothing happens, move to Option-Command-Escape and Force Quit that one app. If the app does not even appear in the Force Quit list, or a background process is the actual problem, open Activity Monitor and end it from there. Reach for a full restart only when the Mac itself has stopped responding to input at all, not as the default first move for a single stuck app. 
 [IMAGE: Warning]
 Holding the power button is not a normal troubleshooting step.
 Holding the power button forces an unclean shutdown of the entire Mac, not just the frozen app, and skips every safety step macOS normally takes when closing files and sessions. Reserve it for when the Mac is completely unresponsive to everything else on this page - not as a shortcut for a single misbehaving plugin window.

wiki_content/macos-p4-ram-storage-and-cp.title: macOS: P4: RAM, Storage, and CPUs
wiki_content/macos-p4-ram-storage-and-cp.text:
macOS: P4: RAM, Storage, and CPUs
 Three components decide how a Mac actually performs under a heavy Pro Tools session: how much temporary workspace it has, how fast it can read and write files, and how quickly it can process instructions. Each one fails differently when it runs short. 
 RAM (Memory)
 RAM is temporary, high-speed workspace the CPU uses while a program runs. It is volatile - everything in it clears the moment the Mac loses power. Every track, plugin, and undo buffer in an open Pro Tools session lives in RAM while you work. 
 Running low on RAM forces macOS to swap data out to the much slower drive to make room, which is exactly when a session starts to stutter or plugins start crackling. Check how much RAM is installed and how much is currently in use from About This Mac, or in detail from Activity Monitor's Memory tab. 
 [IMAGE: System Information's Memory category, showing installed RAM capacity, type, and manufacturer]
 System Information's Memory category goes further than About This Mac - here it shows not just capacity, but the RAM type (LPDDR5) and manufacturer. 
 Storage: Solid State vs. Spinning Disk
 HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
 - spinning magnetic platters read by a moving mechanical arm. Cheaper per gigabyte, but slower, and the moving parts can fail or be damaged by drops and vibration.
 SSD (Solid State Drive)
 - flash memory chips with no moving parts at all. Far faster read and write speeds, and standard in every current Mac.
 Session playback - especially at high track counts, or higher sample rates and bit depths - needs sustained fast read speeds that an HDD can struggle to deliver. An SSD is effectively required for serious session work today. 
 CPUs: PowerPC, Intel, and Apple Silicon
 PowerPC (1994-2006)
 - Apple's original processor architecture, developed with IBM and Motorola. Apple moved away from it when Intel's roadmap offered better performance per watt.
 Intel (2006-2023 transition)
 - the same x86 processor architecture used in Windows PCs - which is also why older Intel Macs could run Windows through Boot Camp.
 Apple Silicon / M-series (2020-present)
 - Apple's own custom-designed chips (M1, M2, M3, M4, and beyond), built on the ARM architecture - the same processor family that powers iPhones and iPads, scaled up for a full Mac.
 [IMAGE: Timeline diagram showing the transition from PowerPC to Intel to Apple Silicon processors]
 Diagram: the three processor generations Apple has shipped, and what changed with each. 
 [IMAGE: Note]
 Unified memory changes the RAM conversation.
 On Apple Silicon Macs, the CPU, GPU, and RAM sit together on one combined chip package, called unified memory. That is why these Macs are dramatically more power-efficient - and also why RAM cannot be upgraded after purchase. It is physically part of the chip, decided at the moment you buy the machine. 
 Rosetta 2
 Rosetta 2 is the translation layer that lets older, Intel-only software keep running on an Apple Silicon Mac, at some performance cost. An old plug-in that has not been updated may run slower under Rosetta, or need to be reinstalled once a Universal build - one that runs natively on both architectures - becomes available. 
 Three Kinds of App, and How to Tell Them Apart
 Native Apple Silicon app
 - built to run directly on ARM, no translation needed, full performance.
 Intel-only app
 - built only for x86, requires Rosetta 2 on an Apple Silicon Mac, and runs slower than it would on the Intel hardware it was written for.
 Universal app
 - contains both an Apple Silicon and an Intel version in one file, and automatically runs the correct one for whichever Mac it is on.
 Select any app in Finder and press Command-I - the Kind field spells out exactly which of the three it is, listed as Application (Intel), Application (Apple Silicon), or Application (Universal). This matters directly for plug-in compatibility: a session full of native, Universal plug-ins runs at full efficiency, while even one Intel-only plug-in in the chain forces that instance through Rosetta, adding CPU overhead that shows up in Activity Monitor's CPU tab. 
 [IMAGE: Tip]
 Tip:
 Pro Tools and most major plug-in vendors now ship Universal builds that run natively on Apple Silicon. If a plug-in still requires Rosetta, expect it to be noticeably less efficient than the rest of the session around it.
 [IMAGE: Get Info window for Pro Tools.app, with the Kind field showing Application (Universal)]
 Pro Tools itself, confirmed as Application (Universal) - it runs natively on both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, no translation layer needed either way. 
 [IMAGE: About This Mac window showing an Apple M5 chip, memory, startup disk, serial number, and macOS version]
 About This Mac - the fastest way to check chip, RAM, and macOS version at a glance. 
 [IMAGE: System Settings General About pane showing the same overview plus connected displays and storage details]
 The same information inside System Settings > General > About, expanded to show connected displays and available storage.

wiki_content/macos-p4-hardware-software-.title: macOS: P4: Hardware, Software, and Firmware
wiki_content/macos-p4-hardware-software-.text:
macOS: P4: Hardware, Software, and Firmware
 These three words get used loosely, but they describe three genuinely different layers of a working computer, and mixing them up leads directly to troubleshooting the wrong thing. 
 Hardware
 Hardware is the physical, touchable equipment - the CPU, the RAM chips, the storage drive, the ports on the side of the Mac, the audio interface sitting on your desk. Hardware cannot be updated with a download; it can only be repaired or replaced. 
 Software
 Software is the set of instructions running on that hardware, from the operating system itself down to a single app. macOS is software. Pro Tools is software. A plugin is software. Software is what gets installed, updated, and uninstalled. 
 Firmware
 Firmware is a special layer of software written directly onto a hardware component itself, controlling how that specific piece of hardware boots and behaves before the operating system ever loads. It usually does not change unless the manufacturer issues a firmware update. 
 Your Mac's own firmware
 - controls the boot process before macOS starts loading at all.
 An audio interface's firmware
 - controls how that interface communicates over USB or Thunderbolt, running on the interface itself - separate entirely from the driver, which is software running on the Mac.
 [IMAGE: Note]
 Why this distinction matters in troubleshooting.
 Reinstalling a driver only changes the software layer running on the Mac. If an interface is behaving oddly, checking the manufacturer's site for a firmware update addresses a completely different layer, and one that a driver reinstall cannot touch. 
 [IMAGE: Layered stack diagram showing Software on top, Firmware in the middle, and Hardware as the base layer]
 Diagram: how the three layers stack on top of each other. 
 A Quick Comparison
 Hardware
 - physical equipment. Updated by replacement, not download.
 Software
 - instructions running on hardware. Installed, updated, and uninstalled freely - macOS, Pro Tools, and every plugin all count.
 Firmware
 - software built into a specific piece of hardware, controlling its lowest-level behavior. Rarely updated, and only through a process the manufacturer provides.

wiki_content/macos-p4-external-drives-vo.title: macOS: P4: External Drives, Volumes, and File Systems
wiki_content/macos-p4-external-drives-vo.text:
macOS: P4: External Drives, Volumes, and File Systems
 Before formatting a drive in Disk Utility, it helps to know what Finder is actually showing you when a drive gets plugged in - the words disk, drive, volume, and partition all mean slightly different things, and mixing them up makes troubleshooting a connection problem harder than it needs to be. 
 Disk, Drive, Volume, and Partition
 Disk / Drive
 - the physical piece of hardware itself - an internal SSD, an external hard drive, a USB stick.
 Volume
 - a formatted, usable storage area that shows up in Finder with its own name and icon. One physical drive can hold one volume, or several.
 Partition
 - the act of splitting one physical drive into multiple separate volumes, each formatted independently.
 Mounting and Ejecting
 Connecting an external drive mounts it automatically - macOS reads its volumes and adds each one to the Finder sidebar with its own eject icon. Always eject a drive before physically disconnecting it, using that icon, Command-E, or dragging its icon to the Trash, which turns into an Eject symbol during the drag. Ejecting flushes any data still waiting to be written and closes out the file system cleanly; unplugging a drive that is mid-write, without ejecting first, is one of the most common causes of a corrupted volume or a Pro Tools session that can no longer be opened. 
 [IMAGE: Finder sidebar showing a real external Time Machine drive mounted alongside the internal Macintosh HD]
 A real external drive - here a Time Machine backup disk - mounted and visible in the sidebar right alongside the internal Macintosh HD. 
 What Disk Utility Does
 Erase
 - wipes a drive and formats it with a file system you choose - this is where you set APFS, exFAT, and the rest.
 Partition
 - splits one physical drive into multiple separate volumes, each with its own file system if needed.
 First Aid
 - checks a drive's directory structure for errors and repairs what it can, without erasing your data.
 Create/mount a disk image
 - builds or opens a DMG - the same disk image format covered on the installers page.
 [IMAGE: Disk Utility showing the Macintosh HD volume, its APFS Startup Snapshot format, capacity, and connection details]
 Disk Utility's info view for a real Macintosh HD volume - APFS Startup Snapshot format, total capacity, and how much is used versus free. 
 [IMAGE: Disk Utility's Erase dialog for a disk image, with Name and Format fields, before choosing a format from the dropdown]
 The Erase dialog - this is exactly where the Format dropdown offers APFS, exFAT, and MS-DOS (FAT) as choices when erasing a real external drive. 
 [IMAGE: Get Info window for the Macintosh HD volume, confirming APFS format, capacity, and available space]
 The same information from a different angle - Get Info (Command-I) on the volume itself confirms Format: APFS without ever opening Disk Utility. 
 A Short History of File Systems
 FAT16
 - the original MS-DOS format from the 1980s, capped around 2GB per volume. No longer used on modern drives.
 FAT32
 - introduced with Windows 95 OSR2. Fixed the volume-size limit, but capped every single file at 4GB. Still shows up today as the default format on SD cards, USB drives, and camera memory.
 exFAT
 - built specifically to replace FAT32 on flash drives. No 4GB file-size limit, and both macOS and Windows read and write it natively - the practical default for a drive shared between the two operating systems.
 NTFS
 - Windows' native, journaled file system since Windows 2000. macOS reads an NTFS drive out of the box but cannot write to it without third-party software.
 HFS+ (Mac OS Extended)
 - Apple's format from 1998 through 2017. Journaled, and case-insensitive by default.
 APFS
 - Apple's current default since 2017, built for flash storage and SSDs. Adds native encryption, near-instant space-efficient snapshots, and stronger crash protection than HFS+. Every new Mac ships formatted this way.
 [IMAGE: Timeline diagram showing FAT16, FAT32, HFS+, NTFS, exFAT, and APFS in chronological order with their introduction years]
 Diagram: a timeline of file systems from FAT16 through APFS. 
 [IMAGE: Warning]
 The 4GB file-size cap is the most common surprise.
 A FAT32-formatted SD card or USB drive will refuse to copy a single exported video or a large session bounce onto it if that file is larger than 4GB - the drive itself is not broken, the file system just cannot hold a file that size. 
 Choosing a Format in Disk Utility
 Mac-only external SSD or drive
 - format as APFS.
 Drive shared between a Mac and a Windows PC
 - format as exFAT.
 Any drive that needs to hold files larger than 4GB
 - never format as FAT32.
 [IMAGE: Tip]
 Tip:
 Run First Aid on a drive first whenever Pro Tools reports that it cannot read or write session files correctly - a directory error is a common, fixable cause.

wiki_content/macos-p4-icloud-cloud-files.title: macOS: P4: iCloud, Cloud Files, and Backup
wiki_content/macos-p4-icloud-cloud-files.text:
macOS: P4: iCloud, Cloud Files, and Backup
 Seeing a file in Finder does not always mean its data is physically sitting on your Mac's drive right now. Understanding the difference - and the separate difference between syncing files and actually backing them up - matters directly for knowing where your session media really lives. 
 Local Files vs. Cloud-Only Files
 A local file's complete data lives on your Mac's own drive, available instantly with no network needed. A cloud-only file has been uploaded to iCloud and then removed from local storage to save space, leaving behind a placeholder that looks identical in Finder but has to be downloaded again before it can actually be opened, played, or edited. 
 Desktop and Documents Syncing
 iCloud Drive can be set to sync your entire Desktop and Documents folders, uploading everything inside them and making that same content available on any other Mac or device signed into the same account. This is convenient, and it is also exactly the setting that most often turns a Pro Tools session folder into a set of cloud-only placeholders without anyone noticing until playback fails. 
 [IMAGE: Finder Settings General tab, showing the Sync Desktop and Documents folders toggle, currently switched off]
 Finder Settings > General - the Sync Desktop & Documents folders toggle lives right here, off by default on this particular Mac. 
 Reading the Cloud Status Icons
 Finder marks cloud-affected files with small icons next to their names: a small cloud with a down arrow means the file is cloud-only and needs downloading before use, and a small clock or spinning icon means it is actively syncing. A file with neither icon is fully local and available immediately. 
 [IMAGE: A Finder list showing a cloud-download icon next to Preview, indicating that folder is not fully stored locally]
 The cloud-download icon next to Preview - everything else in this list is fully local, but this one item needs to be downloaded before it can actually be opened. 
 [IMAGE: Critical]
 Know where your session media actually is before you record.
 A Pro Tools session that lives inside a synced Desktop or Documents folder can have its audio files silently evicted to cloud-only status by macOS to save local space. Working directly from a session folder outside of iCloud sync, or on an external drive, avoids this risk entirely. 
 Backup vs. Sync: Not the Same Thing
 Syncing keeps one current copy of a file consistent across multiple devices - change it on one Mac, and the same change appears everywhere else almost immediately. That is exactly the problem: if a file is deleted, corrupted, or overwritten by mistake, sync faithfully propagates that mistake everywhere too. A real backup is a separate, historical copy, kept independent of your current working files, specifically so you can go back to a version from before something went wrong. 
 Time Machine
 Time Machine, configured under System Settings > General > Time Machine, is macOS's built-in backup tool. Once a backup disk is selected, it keeps hourly, daily, and weekly snapshots of your entire drive going back over time, letting you restore an individual file - or your whole system - to a specific point in the past. Check that panel to confirm a backup disk is actually configured; a Mac with no backup disk selected here has no Time Machine history at all, regardless of how much gets synced through iCloud. 
 [IMAGE: Time Machine's restore interface, showing stacked windows of the same Desktop folder going back through past dates]
 Time Machine's actual restore view - each stacked window is the same folder as it existed at an earlier point in time, with a timeline on the right for jumping to a specific date.

wiki_content/macos-p5-audio-midi-setup.h.title: macOS: P5: Audio MIDI Setup
wiki_content/macos-p5-audio-midi-setup.h.text:
macOS: P5: Audio MIDI Setup
 Audio MIDI Setup is the one built-in Mac utility every DAPR student needs to actually open and use, not just know about. It has two entirely separate windows, and knowing MIDI Studio without ever touching Audio Devices means missing the half of this app that controls your actual interface. 
 The Audio Devices Window
 Open Audio MIDI Setup from Applications > Utilities, and make sure the Audio Devices window is the one showing - Window > Show Audio Devices if it is not already in front. This window lists every audio device macOS currently sees, and selecting your interface here reveals exactly how it is configured. 
 Input channels
 - how many separate input sources the interface provides.
 Output channels
 - how many separate output destinations the interface provides.
 Sample rate
 - how many times per second the interface captures or plays audio, set here for the system as a whole.
 Bit depth
 - how much resolution each individual sample carries, also configured here per device.
 Clock source
 - which device is acting as the master timing reference, on interfaces that support more than one clock source.
 System input / System output
 - the two devices macOS itself defaults to for input and output, chosen from the same window.
 [IMAGE: Required]
 This is mandatory - MIDI Studio alone does not satisfy this requirement.
 Open Audio Devices, select your actual connected interface, and screenshot the window with input channels, output channels, and sample rate all visible. 
 [IMAGE: Audio MIDI Setup's Audio Devices window showing a selected device with sample rate options open]
 The Audio Devices window, with the sample rate menu open showing 44,100 Hz through 96,000 Hz - notice the long list of virtual audio devices in the sidebar, from Pro Tools' own Audio Bridge to third-party utilities. 
 Aggregate Devices and Multi-Output Devices
 Aggregate Device
 - combines multiple separate audio interfaces into one single logical device that other apps see as though it were one piece of hardware - useful when you need more total channels than any one interface provides on its own.
 Multi-Output Device
 - routes the same audio out to multiple hardware outputs at once - useful for sending the same signal to both a set of studio monitors and a separate recording input simultaneously.
 Both are built from the + button in the lower-left of the Audio Devices window. Neither one is something this unit requires you to permanently configure, but understanding what each does explains a setup you will eventually encounter in a lab or a session that already has one built. 
 [IMAGE: Warning]
 Combining interfaces means their clocks have to agree.
 An Aggregate Device only works reliably when every interface inside it is set to the same sample rate, and ideally shares a single clock source. Mismatched sample rates between combined devices is the single most common cause of clicks, pops, or drift in an aggregate setup - drift correction, a setting inside the Aggregate Device editor, exists specifically to compensate for small timing differences between devices that cannot share a hardware clock. 
 [IMAGE: Dolby Audio Bridge speaker configuration window showing a 5.1.4 layout with channels assigned to Left, Right, Center]
 A real multi-channel routing example from Dolby Audio Bridge, a virtual audio device - each output channel gets mapped to a specific speaker position. A Multi-Output Device follows the same underlying idea: specific channels routed to specific physical destinations, not just a single stereo pair. 
 MIDI Studio
 MIDI Studio is a separate window from Audio Devices - switch to it with Window > Show MIDI Studio - showing a visual map of every MIDI device and driver macOS currently recognizes, from physical MIDI interfaces to virtual, software-only connections like Bluetooth MIDI and the IAC Driver. It exists to configure MIDI routing specifically, and has nothing to do with audio channel counts or sample rate - the two windows genuinely do not overlap in function. 
 [IMAGE: Audio MIDI Setup's MIDI Studio window showing a grid of connected and virtual MIDI device icons]
 MIDI Studio, showing Bluetooth MIDI devices, network MIDI, the IAC Driver, and physical MIDI interfaces as icons in a grid.
