macOS: P5: Library vs. System - Pro Tools and Your Files
 At the root of the drive, Library and System look like similar folders, but they hold entirely different kinds of content. This page goes past the basics into what actually lives inside them - especially the parts that matter for audio work. 
 Two Different Library Folders, Quickly Recapped
 /Library
 - visible in Finder by default, shared by every account on the Mac.
 ~/Library
 - hidden by default, and scoped to your own user account only. Reveal it from the Finder Go menu by holding Option.
 Inside Application Support
 Application Support is where an app stores larger, persistent data that goes beyond a simple settings file - custom presets, templates, caches, license data, and helper-app files. 
 [IMAGE: Finder window showing the Library/Application Support folder with a long list of vendor folders]
 /Library/Application Support, showing one folder per company or piece of software that installed something system-wide. 
 Effectively, this is a shared filing cabinet - one folder per vendor. The per-user version, ~/Library/Application Support, holds the same kind of data but scoped to a single account only. 
 Inside Library/Audio
 Both /Library/Audio and ~/Library/Audio hold the files CoreAudio and CoreMIDI - the audio and MIDI engines built into macOS - actually use: 
 Plug-Ins/Components
 - Audio Unit (AU) format plug-ins.
 Plug-Ins/VST and VST3
 - VST-format plug-ins, stored alongside the AU folder.
 MIDI Drivers
 - drivers for MIDI interfaces.
 Sounds
 - system alert sound files.
 Apple Loops
 - loop content used by GarageBand and Logic.
 [IMAGE: Finder window showing the real contents of Library/Audio, including VST XMLs, Sounds, Presets, Plug-Ins]
 Library/Audio on a real, actively-used Mac - considerably more than the short list above once every plug-in and driver installer has added its own folder. 
 This is the actual, physical home of every plug-in a DAW can load. If a plug-in is not showing up in Pro Tools, checking whether its files genuinely exist inside this folder is a direct, filesystem-level check - separate from anything a driver or a Launch Agent controls. 
 Pro Tools' AAX Plug-In Location
 AAX is Avid's own plug-in format, built specifically for Pro Tools, and it lives in a specific, dedicated location rather than the general Plug-Ins folder covered above: 
 /Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins
 - every AAX plug-in Pro Tools can currently load.
 /Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins (Unused)
 - a holding folder Pro Tools uses when a plug-in is deliberately disabled without being deleted. A plug-in sitting here will not appear in Pro Tools until it is moved back into the main Plug-Ins folder.
 AU and VST/VST3 plug-ins use entirely different locations and formats from AAX - the ones already covered above under Library/Audio - which is why the same plug-in from the same manufacturer sometimes has to be installed once for Pro Tools and separately again for a different DAW. 
 [IMAGE: Required]
 Navigate there yourself using Go to Folder.
 Press Shift-Command-G, type /Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins, and press Return. Screenshot the resulting window showing your installed AAX plug-ins - this reinforces both the Go to Folder skill from earlier in this unit and exactly where Pro Tools' plug-ins actually live. 
 [IMAGE: Go to Folder navigating to Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins]
 Go to Folder navigating straight to the AAX Plug-Ins folder, with dozens of real .aaxplugin files visible - and the neighboring Plug-Ins (Unused) and Plug-Ins - Archive folders mentioned above, right where this page says they would be. 
 Pro Tools: User Files vs. System-Wide Files
 Pro Tools itself is the clearest real example of the /Library vs. ~/Library split covered throughout this unit. Its AAX plug-ins, covered above, live in /Library - shared by every account on the Mac, since any user should be able to load the same plug-ins. Pro Tools' own preferences, custom key command sets, and per-user settings, on the other hand, live inside ~/Library/Application Support and ~/Library/Preferences - scoped to your account alone, so two different logins on the same Mac can each have their own personalized Pro Tools setup without interfering with each other. 
 This is not a trivia detail specific to one app - it is the same system-wide-vs-personal split every piece of software on the Mac follows, just made concrete with software you will use every day in this program.

[IMAGE: Required]

Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
Sample rate and bit depthCommitted in the Dashboard when the session is created. Changing them later means converting every file, so get them right once.
Clip gainPre-fader. Use it to even out a performance before the compressor sees it, so the compressor is not fixing something clip gain should have.
Track input trimSets how hot the signal arrives. Aim for peaks well under 0 dBFS; headroom costs nothing and clipping costs a take.

In-Class Mixing: A Repeatable Order of Operations
[IMAGE: Note] 
The order exists so you stop rediscovering it. Session prep, comp, balance, correct, shape, place, glue, deliver. Every stage assumes the one before it is finished. Skipping ahead is why mixes stall. 
[IMAGE: Five-step flow showing the order of a mix pass]

These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
Pass 1, balanceFaders only, no processing, until the arrangement reads.
Pass 2, subtractiveRemove what is in the way before adding anything. Usually low-mid buildup.
Pass 3, dynamicsControl what moves too much, only where it moves too much.
Pass 4, placementPan, depth, reverb and delay. Put things somewhere on purpose.
Pass 5, automationFix the sections the static mix cannot serve.
[IMAGE: Checklist] 
Run the same pass every time. Working in a fixed order turns mixing into a procedure you can finish rather than a mood you have to be in. It is also what lets you pick a session back up after two weeks.

[IMAGE: Note] 
Your room is part of your signal chain. Between the speaker and your ear, the room adds reflections, cancellations and a bass response that can swing 15 dB across two feet of listening position. You are mixing that, whether you meant to or not. 
[IMAGE: Overhead plan of a control room with first reflection paths traced]
Figure 1. The four first reflection points at the mix position. These arrive milliseconds after the direct sound and comb with it.
These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
First reflectionsSound reaching you off a nearby surface a few milliseconds after the direct sound. Causes comb filtering at the listening position.
Modal regionBelow roughly 300 Hz in a small room, the room itself resonates. This is where rooms lie the most.
AbsorptionConverts sound energy to heat. Broadband absorption needs depth; thin foam only touches the top octaves.
DiffusionScatters energy rather than removing it. Keeps a room lively without the specular reflections.
Listening positionWhere all of this is measured and the only place the room is correct.
[IMAGE: Warning] 
Bass is the part the room ruins first. Room modes live below about 300 Hz. If your low end changes when you lean forward six inches, you cannot trust anything you decide about the kick and bass until you fix the position or check on another system. 
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Find the first reflection points before you buy anything. Have someone slide a mirror along the side wall while you sit in the mix position. Anywhere you can see a speaker in the mirror is a first reflection point. That is where absorption goes, and it is the cheapest improvement available.

wiki_content/calibration-speaker-and-hea.text:
Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
When you set up and calibrate speakers, there are three things to worry about: loudness, frequency response, and phase. This page covers loudness only. Once your monitoring system is calibrated for loudness, every mixing decision you make is based on a level you can trust and repeat. 
Why Loudness Calibration Matters
If you monitor too loud, your mix will end up too quiet. 
If you monitor too quiet, your mix will end up too loud. 
If you do not pay attention to your monitoring level at all, you will deliver inconsistent mixes to your clients. 
The Six Gain Stages
Loudness is controlled at six possible points between your DAW and your ears. Two of these stages change the actual audio in your final mix file. The other four only change how loud that file sounds to you in the room, without touching the file itself. 
Channel Fader
The volume fader on an individual channel of a DAW. It controls the volume of a single instrument or vocal performance inside the mix. 
[IMAGE: Required] Affects the final mix: changing this fader changes the sound of your bounced mix file. 
Master Fader
The volume control for the master bus of a DAW. It is the final gain stage before the mix file is created and, on most sessions, is the last thing you would ever touch. It almost never moves except to automate a fade-out. 
[IMAGE: Required] Affects the final mix: changing this fader changes the sound of your bounced mix file. 
Computer Volume
The volume fader of the computer you are working on. If you are listening on headphones plugged directly into the computer, this is likely the last gain stage before your ears. 
[IMAGE: Note] Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself. 
Interface
The output volume control on the interface you are using. This is sometimes a knob on the front of the interface, and it is sometimes controlled digitally through software. It functions like a small monitor section, similar to what you would find on an analog console. 
[IMAGE: Note] Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself. 
Monitor Controller
A device used to control the volume of studio monitors, often across multiple monitor sets at the press of a button. Some units control stereo pairs only. Others handle 5.1, 7.1, or full Dolby Atmos systems, and a well-equipped monitor controller can manage volume, signal processing, phase, and delay across more than 64 separate monitor signals at once. 
[IMAGE: Note] Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself. 
Amplifier Volume
The volume control on the amplifiers connected directly to your speakers. Active (powered) speakers have the amplifier built in. Passive (unpowered) speakers receive power from a separate amplifier. Every speaker that carries a discrete signal should have its own power amplifier. 
[IMAGE: Note] Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself.

Calibrating Your Speakers
Once you know which controller you are using for overall volume, follow these steps. 
Decide how you want to control your overall speaker volume. 
Send a test signal through the system. 
Measure the signal coming out of the speakers with an SPL meter, or your ears once you are experienced enough. 
Adjust the power amplifiers of your speakers so each speaker sits at the same volume and at a good level. 
Mark or note where your overall speaker volume controller is set so you can return to that position. 
Do not touch any other gain stage again, unless you are calibrating it again. 
Choosing a Test Signal
Send one of the following through your system to calibrate against. 
Music
Choose a song that is well mixed and holds a consistent level throughout. Frequency content and overall loudness vary greatly between songs, which makes music the least reliable of the three test signals. 
Pink Noise (-20 dB)
Noise with equal energy per octave. It is a full-range signal that works well for measuring average loudness. 
M Noise (-20 dB)
Developed by Meyer Sound, M Noise carries more of the qualities of real music than pink noise does. Learn more at m-noise.org (opens in a new tab). 
Measuring the Signal
Use an SPL meter when you can get one. Phone-based SPL metering apps work as a backup, though results vary between apps and devices. 
Here is the math behind the target level: if you want 20 dB of headroom, your test signal averages -20 dBFS, and your speakers are rated for 105 dB SPL or higher, aim for 85 dB SPL on your meter at the mix position. 
[IMAGE: Note] Test one speaker at a time. Confirm both speakers measure exactly the same before moving on.

Adjusting the Power Amplifiers
If your signal reads too soft or too loud, adjust the power amplifiers until each speaker matches the target level of 85 dB SPL. Send signal to one speaker at a time, and confirm both speakers measure exactly the same before you finish. 
Marking Your Calibrated Position
Mark or note where your chosen main volume controller sits at your calibrated level, so you can return to that exact position every time. 
[IMAGE: Warning] Not every monitor controller reads actual SPL. Some let you set the dial to show the real SPL at the mix position, so a dial reading of 85 dB truly means 85 dB in the room. Many are not that precise. Either way, mark or note where 85 dB SPL falls on your dial. 
Do Not Touch Any Other Gain Stage Again
[IMAGE: Critical] Changing the amplifier volume breaks your calibration. Use only the controller you designated as the main controller to adjust volume. Use your 85 dB mark as an anchor so you always know where you stand. 
Mixing at 85 dB is too loud for many projects, and that is fine. To find a comfortable working level, choose a piece of music that matches the style and loudness you are aiming for and play it through your system. Turn the main level down until it feels comfortable, then mark that new position so you know exactly what to return to. 
Establishing a Headphone Reference Listening Level
You cannot hold a standard SPL meter up to a headphone driver and get a meaningful loudspeaker-style measurement. The pressure at your eardrum depends on the enclosed ear volume, pad seal, headphone placement, your pinna, and your ear canal, none of which a handheld meter accounts for. Genuine standardized headphone measurement requires an acoustic coupler, ear simulator, or HATS (head and torso simulator) system under IEC 60268-7. 
[IMAGE: Critical] A handheld SPL meter is not a valid way to calibrate headphones to an absolute SPL. 
Three ways to set a headphone listening level, from least to most rigorous
Method
What It Establishes
Good For

The standard classroom method used in this course

Lab, research, and manufacturer testing
Loudness-Matching Method
This course uses the loudness-matching approach described in ITU-R BS.1116: calibrate your monitors first, then match the headphones to that calibrated sound field by ear. 
Set the DAW master output to unity gain. 
Load a standardized pink noise calibration signal at a known digital level. 
Calibrate your loudspeaker reference level with an SPL meter, following the speaker calibration steps above. 
Sit in the calibrated listening position and listen to the pink noise through the monitors. 
Switch to the headphones without changing the digital signal level. 
Adjust only the headphone amplifier or headphone output level until the headphones sound approximately equal in loudness to the calibrated monitors. 
Switch between the monitors and the headphones several times to refine the match. 
Mark or record the headphone level setting. This is your headphone reference listening level. 
Return to this reference level regularly while working, even though you will monitor quieter or louder at times. Spend most of your working time at moderate levels and keep louder checks brief. 
[IMAGE: Note] The reference chain, in order: -18 dBFS pink noise, calibrated monitors at 78 dBA, headphones matched by ear to the monitors, then the headphone level marked as your reference. 
There is no universal 85 dB SPL headphone standard equivalent to loudspeaker calibration practice. The 78 dBA figure above comes from the loudspeaker reference level in ITU-R BS.1116 and EBU Tech 3276, not from a headphone-specific target. The lesson here is the distinction between digital reference level, acoustic reference level, monitor calibration, and subjective loudness, not a single magic number. 
[IMAGE: Tip] Do not confuse this with hearing-safety guidance. ITU-T H.870 recommends 80 dBA for up to 40 hours a week as a safe listening exposure limit. That is a hearing-safety recommendation, not a mixing calibration target. 
Ear Simulator / HATS Measurement
Actual measured headphone SPL requires calibrated hardware. This is beyond the equipment used in this course, but you should know the procedure exists: calibrate a measurement microphone or ear simulator appropriate to the headphone type, seat the headphone on the fixture per the measurement procedure, play a defined calibration signal at a defined digital level, measure each channel separately, adjust the headphone amplifier to the target acoustic output, and reseat the headphones several times since pad position and seal materially affect the reading. Record the headphone model, interface, amplifier setting, test signal level, measurement weighting, fixture, and measured SPL. IEC 60268-7 is the current standard for headphone and earphone measurement, and the IEC 60318 family defines the ear and head simulators used to perform it. 
[IMAGE: Ear cross section with a headphone cup sealed, beside one with the seal broken and sound escaping]
Figure 1. A broken seal loses the low end first. Glasses, long hair and a worn earpad all cost you bass you will then try to fix in the mix.
[IMAGE: Head in profile with a measurement microphone at the eardrum feeding a response plot]
Figure 2. How headphone response is actually measured. The microphone sits where your eardrum would be, which is why published curves differ between labs.

wiki_content/calibration-reference-noise.text:
Calibration: Reference Noise Files
[IMAGE: Headphone Seal Cross Section]
Figure 1. Headphone Seal Cross Section.
Two calibration files are provided below for use in the Core Mixing studio: a pink noise reference and an M Noise reference. Both are used to check that your monitoring level is set correctly before you start a mix, but they are not interchangeable, and understanding why matters for anyone doing critical listening work. 
[IMAGE: Download] Download the calibration files:
Calibration-PinkNoise-48kHz-24bit.wav (24-bit / 48kHz, ~31 seconds) 
Calibration-MNoise-96kHz-16bit.wav (16-bit / 96kHz, ~53 seconds) 
Why We Do Not Use White Noise
White noise carries equal energy at every frequency on a linear scale. That sounds like a fair, neutral test signal, but human hearing and most acoustic measurement do not work on a linear frequency scale, they work in octaves. Each time you go up an octave, the number of frequencies packed into that octave doubles. Since white noise has equal energy per frequency, an octave with twice as many frequencies in it ends up with twice as much total energy. The practical result is that white noise sounds like it is getting louder and brighter as you go up in pitch, roughly 3 dB per octave. That tilt makes it a poor reference for anything involving level matching, speaker calibration, or perceived tonal balance, because the signal itself is not tonally neutral to begin with. 
Pink Noise
Pink noise corrects for the octave problem by shaping the spectrum so that energy is equal per octave rather than equal per frequency. That means the low octaves and the high octaves each carry the same total power, which matches how we perceive loudness across the frequency range far better than white noise does. This is why pink noise became the long-standing standard for setting monitor levels, checking speaker balance left to right, and doing basic room response checks with an SPL meter. It sounds noticeably darker than white noise, closer to a steady rushing or hissing sound with the harshness rolled off the top end. 
Pink noise still has a limitation for modern calibration work. Real program material, especially music and dialogue, is not a smooth, static full-spectrum signal the way pink noise is. Pink noise can make a room or a set of speakers look calibrated on paper while still leaving level-matching judgments during actual mixing sessions feeling inconsistent. 
M Noise
M Noise is a newer calibration signal developed specifically to address that gap. Instead of a smooth, unchanging spectrum, M Noise is built from real musical program material that has been processed to retain the statistical loudness and crest-factor characteristics of actual music while remaining repeatable and measurable like a test tone. It was developed through research aimed at large-format sound reinforcement and cinema calibration, and it has increasingly replaced pink noise as the reference signal of choice for loudspeaker and room calibration where the goal is matching what a system will actually sound like under real program material, not just a synthetic average. 
[IMAGE: Tip] Tip:
If you see a plugin or a piece of gear referencing "M Noise" and are not sure what it means, it is not a typo for "pink noise." It is a distinct, purpose-built signal with a different statistical structure. 
Other Noise Colors You Might Encounter
Pink and white are the two you will use most often in this program, but the "noise color" naming system extends further, borrowed from the same visible-light spectrum analogy that gives pink noise its name. 
Brown noise (also called red noise) - falls off at 6 dB per octave, twice as steep as pink noise. It sounds deep and rumbling, closer to a low waterfall or distant thunder. The name references Brownian motion, the random-walk process it is mathematically derived from, rather than the color brown itself. Occasionally used for testing subwoofer and low-frequency extension. 
Blue noise - the inverse of pink noise, rising at 3 dB per octave. It sounds thin and hissy, weighted heavily toward the high end. Used in some dithering algorithms because ear sensitivity to that kind of high-frequency noise shaping is comparatively low. 
Violet noise (also called purple noise) - rises at 6 dB per octave, the mirror image of brown noise. Extremely bright and harsh. Sometimes used to test tweeter response or to analyze quantization noise, since quantization error itself tends to have a violet-like spectrum. 
Gray noise - white noise that has been reshaped using an equal-loudness contour, so that it is perceptually flat to human hearing rather than mathematically flat across frequency. It sounds smoother and less harsh than white noise for the same reason pink noise does, but the correction curve is based on psychoacoustic loudness perception rather than the octave-energy math pink noise uses. 
Other Common Test Signals
A few additional signals show up often enough in calibration and testing work that they are worth knowing by name, even though they are not part of the noise-color family. 
Pure tones (sine sweeps) - a single frequency, or a sweep through a range of frequencies, used to measure the response of a specific speaker, room mode, or piece of gear at precise points rather than across the whole spectrum at once. 
Reference tones (1 kHz, -18 dBFS or -20 dBFS) - a steady single-frequency tone at a defined digital level, used to align meter calibration between different pieces of gear or different rooms, rather than to test frequency response.

Calibration and Monitoring: MS (Mid-Side) Matrix
[IMAGE: Mid side encode and decode signal flow with 0.5 gain stages on both decoded outputs]
Figure 1. Mid is the sum, side is the difference. Everything a mid-side matrix does follows from those two operations.
This page explains the Mid-Side (MS) microphone technique and how to set up the decoding matrix required in Pro Tools Lab 02. Read through this before you start the timer. 
What Is the Mid-Side Technique?
Mid-Side is a coincident stereo microphone technique that records two separate signals: 
Mid (M): A cardioid or omnidirectional microphone pointing directly at the source. This captures the center image. 
Side (S): A figure-8 (bidirectional) microphone positioned at 90 degrees to the Mid mic, with its positive lobe facing left. This captures the difference between left and right. 
Why bother? MS gives you mono-compatible recordings and lets you adjust the stereo width after recording by changing the level of the Side signal. It is widely used in classical, broadcast, and location recording. 
The file 02_Pair_FrontMS in your session is a two-channel interleaved stereo file where the Left channel = Mid and the Right channel = Side. These are raw signals. They cannot be listened to directly as a stereo pair without decoding them first. 
The Decoding Formula
To convert MS into a normal Left/Right stereo pair, you use this matrix: 
MS Decoding Matrix
Output Channel
Formula
What You Hear
Left
Mid + Side
Center plus left-leaning ambience
Center (sum)
Mid only
Pure center image (mono compatible)
Right
Mid - Side
Center plus right-leaning ambience (Side inverted)
[IMAGE: Note] 
Where the x 0.5 in the diagram went. The signal flow figure shows a 0.5 gain stage on each decoded output, because M + S is twice the original Left and the matrix would come back 6 dB hot without it. In the three track build below that job belongs to the Side track faders, which is also how you set the width: pull both Side tracks down together for a narrower image, push them up for a wider one. Keep them matched, or the image pulls to one side. 
The key insight: to create the Right channel, you need a copy of the Side signal with its polarity flipped (inverted). This is why you need to use the EQ 3 polarity invert on one of the Side copies. 
Step 1: Identify the Side Mic in Your Import
When you import the MS file, Pro Tools may create a stereo track with both channels grouped together. Before you can build the matrix, you need to identify which channel is the ambient (Side) mic and which is the Mid. For this assignment the convention is: 
Left channel = Mid mic (cardioid, pointing at the source) 
Right channel = Side mic (figure-8, the ambient mic capturing the stereo difference signal) 
Solo the stereo track and listen to each channel individually using the channel solo buttons in the Mix window to confirm which is which before you split. The Side mic will sound diffuse and ambient with an unusual phase character, it is not meant to be listened to alone. 
Step 2: Split the Stereo Track into Two Mono Tracks
A stereo track in Pro Tools keeps both channels locked together. To work with Mid and Side independently you need to break the track into separate mono tracks. 
Select the stereo track in the Edit window. 
Go to Track > Split Into Mono. Pro Tools creates two new mono tracks, one for the left channel and one for the right channel. 
The original stereo track remains. Mute it or delete it, you will work exclusively from the two new mono tracks. 
Rename the two new tracks immediately. If they came in with generic names, rename them now: the left-channel track is your Mid track, the right-channel track is your Side track. Clear naming here prevents confusion in every step that follows. 
Note: After a Split Into Mono, Pro Tools appends .L and .R to the original track name. Rename both tracks before continuing. Generic names like 02_Pair_FrontMS.L will cause confusion when you duplicate the Side track in the next step. 
Step 3: Duplicate the Side Track
The matrix requires two copies of the Side signal: one for the Left decode and one for the Right decode (polarity inverted). Duplicate the Side track to create the second copy. 
Select your Side track in the Edit window. 
Press Option + Shift + D (Mac) to open the Duplicate Track dialog. 
In the dialog, make sure Playlist is checked (it is the first option). This carries the audio regions across to the duplicate. Leave Insert After Last Selected Track checked so it lands in a logical position. 
Click OK. You now have two Side tracks. Rename them clearly: one will become MS L (Side normal) and the other will become MS R (Side inverted). 
Tip: If Playlist is not checked in the Duplicate Track dialog, the new track will be empty. It creates the track structure but does not copy the audio regions. Always verify Playlist is checked before clicking OK. 
Step 4: Build the Three Matrix Tracks
You should now have three mono tracks. Rename and configure each one as follows: 
02 - MS L: The Side track (normal polarity). Pan hard left. This track carries the Side signal only. Panned hard left it sums with the centred Mid track, and that sum is Mid + Side at the left output. No polarity invert. 
03 - MS C: The Mid track. Pan center. This track carries only the Mid signal = Center output. No polarity invert. 
04 - MS R: The duplicate Side track. Pan hard right. Insert EQ 3 1-Band and activate the polarity invert button. This track carries the inverted Side signal only. Panned hard right it sums with the centred Mid track, and that sum is Mid minus Side at the right output. 
Note: Polarity invert is not the same as phase shift. Polarity invert flips the entire waveform 180 degrees at all frequencies simultaneously. This is what MS decoding requires. A phase shift plug-in would be incorrect here. 
Step 5: Mix Group the Side Tracks
Tracks MS L and MS R are both derived from the Side mic. They should always move together in level so the stereo decode stays balanced. Create a Mix Group for just these two tracks so their faders move together. 
Select tracks MS L and MS R in the Mix or Edit window (Command-click to select both). 
Press Command + G to open the Create Group dialog. 
Set the Group Type to Mix (not Edit, and not Mix/Edit, you only need fader control here). Name the group MS Sides or similar. 
Make sure Main Volume is checked under the attributes. Click OK. 
With this group active, raising or lowering either Side track fader moves both simultaneously. This lets you adjust the width of the MS decode (more Side = wider, less Side = narrower) without unbalancing left and right. 
Step 6: Place the Three Tracks in a Routing Folder
Put the three MS tracks (MS L, MS C, MS R) into a routing folder to keep the session organized and to provide a single bus for feeding the rest of the mix. 
Select all three MS tracks. 
Go to Track > Create Folder Track (or drag the tracks into an existing folder). Name the folder MS. 
A routing folder routes the output of all tracks inside it through a single bus. This gives you a master fader for the entire MS group, useful for riding the overall level of the pair against the rest of the session. 
Why Three Tracks Instead of Two?
Standard MS decode produces a Left and Right stereo pair, two outputs. This assignment asks for three tracks (MS L, MS C, MS R) because it gives you independent control over each decoded element: 
MS L panned hard left, carries the Left decode 
MS C panned center, carries only the Mid signal, reinforcing the center image 
MS R panned hard right, carries the Right decode (Side inverted) 
This three-track layout lets you adjust stereo width in real time by changing the level of MS L and MS R relative to MS C. It is a common approach in classical music post-production. 
Quick Verification
After setting up the matrix, run these checks before moving on to the next task: 
Solo MS C and listen. You should hear a clear, stable center image with no stereo spread. If it sounds wide, the routing is incorrect. 
Sum MS L and MS R together (both soloed). If the Side signal is correctly inverted, the Side components cancel and you are left with only the Mid signal, the same as MS C alone. 
Confirm the EQ 3 polarity invert button is lit (active) on MS R only. If it is active on MS L or MS C by mistake, your decode will be wrong. 
Volume Levels for the MS Tracks
After decoding, set these fader levels on your three MS tracks:

wiki_content/dynamic-effects-compression.text:
Dynamic Effects: Compression, The Seven Controls
[IMAGE: Hand lettered board listing six rules of compression with a sketch under each one]
Figure 1. Six rules worth having in your head before you touch a single control.
[IMAGE: Note] 
Seven controls, one question. Threshold, ratio, attack, release, knee, makeup and side-chain all exist to answer one thing: what should this track do when it gets loud. Decide that first and the settings follow. 
[IMAGE: Dyn3 Compressor and Limiter control panel]
Figure 2. The Dyn3 Compressor and Limiter panel. Ratio, Threshold, Attack, Knee, Release, Depth and Gain are the seven controls every compression decision comes down to.
These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
ThresholdThe level above which compression happens. Everything else is a response to this.
RatioHow hard it compresses above threshold. 2:1 is gentle shaping, 10:1 and above is limiting.
AttackHow fast it clamps down. Fast attack catches the transient, slow attack lets it through.
ReleaseHow fast it lets go. Too fast pumps, too slow and the next note arrives still compressed.
KneeHow abruptly the ratio engages around the threshold. Soft knee for transparency, hard knee for control.
Makeup gainPuts back what compression took. Always compare at matched loudness.
Gain reduction meterThe only control that tells you the truth. Watch it more than you watch the knobs.
[IMAGE: Warning] 
A fast attack is not a safe default. Attack times under about 3 ms clamp the transient, which is the part that tells a listener a drum was hit. If the kick went soft after you patched the compressor in, the attack is too fast. 
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Set release by the tempo. Let the gain reduction meter return to zero just before the next hit. If the needle never comes back, the release is too slow and the track is being held down continuously instead of being shaped. 
[IMAGE: Two gain reduction traces over one kick pattern, one dipping deeply per hit, one barely moving]
Figure 3. The same compressor on the same source. Above, no side chain filter and the kick drives the whole gain reduction. Below, a high pass at 100 Hz on the detector and the pumping is gone.

Spectral Effects and EQ: Why We Use Equalization
[IMAGE: Note] 
EQ is a decision, not a habit. Every move you make should answer a question you asked first. "The vocal is buried" is a question. "I always high-pass at 80" is a habit. 
[IMAGE: 304E Equalizer plugin window showing Bass, Mid, Mid Freq, Treble and Gain controls]
Figure 1. The 304E Equalizer. Bass, Mid and Treble with a sweepable Mid Frequency, which is enough to hear what a broad tonal move does before reaching for a surgical filter.
Equalization, often shortened to EQ, is the process of changing the level of specific frequency ranges in audio so that the sound is clearer, more balanced, and more appropriate for the listening context. 
Core Reasons We EQ
We EQ to improve clarity by reducing frequency buildup that masks important detail in a voice, instrument, or mix. 
We EQ to shape tone by emphasizing or softening parts of the spectrum that influence how something feels, such as warmth, presence, or brightness. 
We EQ to solve problems by reducing resonances, harshness, rumble, or boomy frequencies that distract from the intended sound. 
We EQ to make multiple tracks fit together by carving space so each element can be heard without competing in the same frequency range. 
We EQ to match a target by adjusting a recording or mix so it translates better across different playback systems, rooms, and listeners. 
EQ Goals in Plain Language
We EQ to remove what is not helping the sound. 
We EQ to highlight what matters most in the sound. 
We EQ to help the listener understand and emotionally connect with what they are hearing. 
Two Common EQ Approaches
Corrective EQ focuses on fixing issues like boxiness, muddiness, harshness, hum, rumble, and resonant ringing. 
Tonal EQ focuses on shaping character, such as adding warmth, adding presence, or smoothing brightness for a more polished sound. 
When EQ Is Not the Best First Move
If the source is wrong, we often get better results by changing the instrument, the player, the microphone choice, or the microphone placement. 
If the room is causing problems, we often get better results by changing the position in the room, adding absorption, or reducing reflective surfaces. 
If the level balance is off, we often get better results by adjusting faders before reaching for EQ. 
Interactive Parametric EQ Reference
Use this interactive tool to explore how a parametric equalizer affects the sound, including frequency, gain, and Q (bandwidth). 
 Interactive Parametric EQ Tool (Webtet) 
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Cut before you boost. Cutting the frequency that is in the way costs no headroom and changes no tone anywhere else. Boosting the frequency you want raises the whole track and usually needs the fader pulled back anyway. 
[IMAGE: Avoid] 
Do not EQ in solo. A track soloed has nothing to be masked by, so every problem you hear in solo is a problem that may not exist in the mix. Judge the move in context, every time. 
[IMAGE: Two overlapping spectra summing muddy, beside the same two carved apart summing clear]
Figure 2. Left, both sources fight for the same band and the sum goes muddy. Right, one is cut where the other lives, and both are audible.

wiki_content/spectral-effects-and-eq-fil.text:
Spectral Effects and EQ: Filter Shapes and What They Are For
[IMAGE: Note] 
The shape is the decision. A bell fixes one problem. A shelf changes a whole region. A high-pass removes what was never wanted. Picking the wrong shape is a bigger error than picking the wrong frequency. 
[IMAGE: 304E Equalizer plugin window showing Bass, Mid, Mid Freq, Treble and Gain controls]
Figure 1. The 304E Equalizer. Bass, Mid and Treble with a sweepable Mid Frequency, which is enough to hear what a broad tonal move does before reaching for a surgical filter.
These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
High-pass filterRemoves energy below a corner frequency. The most useful filter in a mix and the easiest to overuse.
Low shelfLifts or cuts everything below a frequency by a fixed amount. Broad tonal shaping.
Bell, or peakingBoosts or cuts around a center frequency. Q sets how wide.
QNarrow Q for surgical cuts, wide Q for musical shaping. A narrow boost almost always sounds worse than a wide one.
High shelfAir and presence, or the opposite. Gentler than a bell for top-end work.
[IMAGE: Tip] 
High-pass with your eyes shut. Sweep the high-pass up until the track thins, then back it off until it is full again. The point where it thinned is what the track actually needed, not 80 Hz because that is the number everyone repeats. 
[IMAGE: Avoid] 
Narrow Q is for problems, not for tone. A Q above about 4 is a scalpel for a resonance or a ring. Using it to shape tone leaves a notch that follows the track through every arrangement change and sounds wrong on half of them. 
[IMAGE: Frequency plot from 20 Hz to 20 kHz with a broad gentle boost and a deep narrow cut]
Figure 2. Boost wide, cut narrow. A broad lift sounds like tone. A narrow notch sounds like a problem being removed, which is what you want it to sound like.

Frequency Dynamics and Side-Chains: Procedure Guide
[IMAGE: Required] 
Follow this in order. Each step assumes the one before it is complete. If a step will not work, the cause is almost always something skipped earlier, not the step you are on. 
[IMAGE: Pro Compressor with the side-chain section open and an external key input selected]
Figure 1. Pro Compressor with its Side-Chain section open. The Source menu is set to an external bus, which is how one track ends up controlling the compression on another.
Use this self-contained guide before completing the assignment work in this module. It explains the operating workflow; the corresponding assignment provides the required project-specific settings and submission evidence. 
The Signal Path, Before You Touch a Control
A side-chain is two signal paths, not one. The trigger track does the pushing. A key send carries a copy of it to the side chain input on the compressor, and the compressor, inserted on the ducked track, turns that key signal into gain reduction. You never hear the trigger through the compressor; you hear the ducked track dip each time the trigger hits. Read the diagram in number order before you open a single menu. 
[IMAGE: Trigger track sent to a compressor side chain input, ducked track dipping on each hit]
Figure 2. The trigger track (1) feeds a key send (2) into the side chain input (3). The compressor (4) sits on the ducked track, and its output (5) dips each time the trigger hits.
The five numbered points in the diagram, in signal order
1Trigger track (the kick or voice that does the pushing)
2Key send off the trigger track
3Side chain (key) input on the compressor
4The compressor, inserted on the ducked track
5The compressor's output: its gain reduction pulls the ducked track down each time the trigger hits
In Pro Compressor, point 3 is the Source menu in the Side-Chain section, shown in the screenshot at the top of this page. Set it to the bus the key send feeds, not to the ducked track's own signal. 
Step-by-Step Workflow
Identify the masking relationship and decide which source should trigger control of the other source. 
Insert a dynamics processor on the controlled track, enable its key input, and route the trigger source to that key or side-chain bus. 
Filter the key signal when needed so only the frequency range causing the conflict drives gain reduction. 
Adjust threshold, ratio, attack, and release while listening to the full mix. Confirm that gain reduction occurs only when the trigger is present.

wiki_content/frequency-dynamics-and-side.text:
Frequency Dynamics and Side-Chains: How They Work
[IMAGE: Note] 
A side-chain is a compressor listening to something else. The audio you hear and the audio that triggers the gain reduction do not have to be the same signal. That one idea covers ducking, de-essing and frequency selective control. 
[IMAGE: Pro Compressor with the side-chain section open and an external key input selected]
Figure 1. Pro Compressor with its Side-Chain section open. The Source menu is set to an external bus, which is how one track ends up controlling the compression on another.
These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
Key inputThe signal that triggers the compressor, which is not the signal being compressed.
Side-chain filterMakes the compressor listen to only part of the spectrum. A high-pass here stops the kick pumping the whole mix.
Multiband compressionDifferent compression per frequency band. Solves what static EQ cannot, and causes what static EQ never would.
De-esserA compressor keyed to the sibilant range. The same idea, one band, one job.
DuckingUsing one source to pull another down. Voice over music is the obvious case, kick over bass is the useful one.
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Filter the key input first. Before you set threshold, high-pass the key input so the compressor stops reacting to low end you never wanted it to react to. Most of the time that alone fixes the pumping. 
[IMAGE: Warning] 
Kick-triggered bass ducking is easy to overdo. Aim for 2 to 3 dB of reduction with a release that recovers before the next kick. If you can hear the bass breathe as a separate event, it is too much. 
[IMAGE: A kick pattern keying a compressor while a bass part dips on every kick]
Figure 2. The kick never passes through the compressor. It only tells the compressor when to pull the bass down, which is why the two stop fighting.

wiki_content/balancing-and-reverb-placin.text:
Balancing and Reverb: Placing a Source in a Space
[IMAGE: Note] 
What reverb is actually for. Reverb does not make a track sound better. It puts the track somewhere. Before you open D-Verb, decide how far back this source should sit and whether it belongs in the same room as everything else. 
[IMAGE: D-Verb plugin window showing its seven algorithms, pre-delay, decay and diffusion]
Figure 1. D-Verb, with all seven algorithms visible. Note there is no early reflections control: pre-delay, decay, diffusion and HF cut are what you actually shape a space with here.
These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
AlgorithmHall, Church, Plate, Room, Ambient, Non-Linear. Each is a different assumption about the space.
Pre-delayThe gap before the reverb arrives. Longer pre-delay keeps the source forward while still placing it.
DecayHow long the tail lasts. Match it to the tempo, not to taste.
DiffusionHow quickly the reflections smear together. Low diffusion is discrete echoes, high is a wash.
Wet and dry balanceOn a send, this stays fully wet and the send level does the work.
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Set decay to the tempo, not to taste. Play the song and lengthen decay until the tail just clears before the next downbeat. At 120 BPM that is roughly 1.8 seconds. Longer than that and the tail sits on top of the next chord. 
[IMAGE: Avoid] 
One reverb per source is how a mix turns to mud. Use one or two send reverbs the whole mix shares. Eight instances of D-Verb on eight inserts is eight different rooms fighting each other, and no amount of EQ fixes that. 
[IMAGE: Four rooms from small room to cathedral, each with a bar showing pre delay and decay growing]
Figure 2. Bigger room, longer pre delay and longer decay. Pick the space first, then set the two numbers to match it.

Balancing & Reverb: Common Mistakes and How to Hear Them
[IMAGE: Warning] 
These are the errors that cost marks. Every item below has shown up in real student submissions in this course. Read them before you submit, not after you get the grade back. 
[IMAGE: Routing diagram contrasting reverb on an insert with reverb on a send and return]
Figure 1. Reverb on an insert against reverb on a send. The send version gives you one space, many sources, and one fader to control it.
Every one of these is a mistake that gets made in this room every semester. The middle column is the part worth memorizing: what the mistake sounds like is how you catch it in your own work. 
Each mistake, the sound that gives it away, and what to do instead
The mistakeWhat you hearWhat to do instead
Reverb on an insert instead of a sendYou cannot share the space, you cannot balance it, and the dry signal is stuck to it.Put reverb on a send and return. One space, many sources, one fader to control it.
No pre-delayThe source moves backward in the mix and loses its front.Add 20 to 40 ms and hear the source step forward while staying in the space.
Decay that fights the tempoThe tail is still going when the next chord arrives and the mix is mud.Set decay by ear against the tempo, then shorten it until the mix breathes.
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Hearing it is the skill. Each mistake has a listening cue attached. Learn the cue and you stop needing the checklist.

wiki_content/delay-and-stereo-enhancemen.text:
Delay and Stereo Enhancements: Width Without Losing Mono
[IMAGE: Note] 
Width is a trade, not a gift. Every widening trick works by making the two channels different. The more different they are, the more cancels when someone plays the mix on one speaker, which is most phones, most club systems and every laptop. 
[IMAGE: Moogerfooger Analog Delay plugin showing delay time, feedback, drive and mix]
Figure 1. The Moogerfooger Analog Delay. Delay Time, Feedback and Mix are the three that set whether a delay supports the part or competes with it.
These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
Delay timeSet against tempo. A quarter, an eighth or a dotted eighth are starting points, not rules.
FeedbackHow many repeats. More than a few and you are building a texture, not an effect.
Filtering in the repeatsDarker repeats sit behind the source. Full-range repeats compete with it.
Stereo spreadDifference between the channels. Real width comes from difference, not from level.
Mono compatibilityWhatever you do to widen, check it summed. Phase tricks that vanish in mono are not width, they are a gamble.
[IMAGE: Warning] 
Check mono before you commit. Sum the master to mono and listen. If the widened part vanishes or the low end drops, the trick is stealing more than it gives. Narrow it until mono survives. 
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Delay beats a stereo plugin for width. A 15 to 30 ms delay on one side reads as width and mostly survives mono. A stereo imager that phase-inverts the sides does not. 
[IMAGE: Figure of eight with a positive lobe, a negative lobe and a null plane between them]
Figure 2. The side signal is two lobes of opposite polarity with a null between them. Anything arriving on that plane is centre, and disappears from the side channel entirely.

The mistakeWhat you hearWhat to do instead

wiki_content/master-buss-processing-and-.text:
Master-Buss Processing and Endgame: Knowing When to Stop
[IMAGE: Note] 
The master buss is not where a mix gets fixed. If the mix needs 4 dB of master buss EQ, the problem is on a channel. Go back and find it. Master buss processing is for the last few percent, after the mix already works. 
[IMAGE: Channel Strip plugin window showing EQ curve, dynamics graph and filter section]
Figure 1. Channel Strip, showing the EQ curve and the dynamics graph in one window. On a master buss every move here should be small enough to argue for.
These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to. 
Each control and what it does
ControlWhat it does
Master faderPost everything. Leave it at unity and control level upstream.
Buss compressionSmall amounts. 1 to 2 dB of gain reduction on the mix buss is a lot.
Buss EQBroad moves only. If you need a narrow cut on the master, it belongs on a track.
LimitingFor control, not for loudness, at this stage. Mastering is a different job with different ears.
Headroom on deliveryLeave the peaks under 0 dBFS. What you deliver is not what a streaming service will play back.
[IMAGE: Warning] 
Leave headroom on delivery. Print with peaks around -6 dBFS and no limiter on the master unless the assignment asks for one. Mastering needs room to work, and a mix squashed flat gives it none. 
[IMAGE: Tip] 
How to know you are done. You are done when your next three moves are all under 1 dB and you cannot say which one helped. Bounce it, leave it a day, and listen once in the car. If you still want to change something, it will be obvious in the first ten seconds.

wiki_content/presentations-and-sessions-.text:
Presentations and Sessions: Building a Ten Minute Presentation
3 Credit(s)  |  Digital Media Audio Production  |  Utah Valley University 
[IMAGE: Core Mixing Lab DAPR 2020L course card]
Figure 1. Core Mixing Lab, DAPR 2020L, the lab half of this course.
The presentation is worth 100 points and it is ten minutes. That is short. The single most common failure is running out of time before you have played the second mix, which means the audience never hears the thing the whole talk exists to show. 
A shape that fits in ten minutesA ten minute running order that leaves room for both mixes
TimeWhat is happening
0:00 to 1:00Name the song, the problem you set out to solve, and what you want us listening for. No history, no apologies.
1:00 to 3:00Play the week 05 version. Do not talk over it. Let the room hear what you started with.
3:00 to 5:00Play the week 13 version of the same material. Same level, same playback system, no talking.
5:00 to 8:00Walk through the three decisions that made the difference, in the order you made them. Show the session or the plug-in for each one.
8:00 to 10:00What you would do next if you had another week, and questions.
Level match before you present, not duringBounce both versions, load them into a session side by side, and match their loudness before you walk into the room. An A and B where one is two decibels louder is not a comparison, it is a loudness test, and the louder one always wins. Match them and the actual differences become audible. 
What to bringBoth bounces as files on a drive, not streamed and not in a cloud folder you have to log in to reach. A session you can open if someone asks to see a specific move. Nothing else. Slides are optional and usually get in the way of listening. 
Talking while audio playsDo not. The room cannot listen to a mix and to you at the same time, and the mix is what you are being graded on. Say what to listen for, play it, then talk.

wiki_content/presentations-and-sessions-.text:
Presentations and Sessions: Common Mistakes and How to Hear Them
3 Credit(s)  |  Digital Media Audio Production  |  Utah Valley University 
[IMAGE: Session delivery package contents laid out]
Figure 1. A delivery package: one project folder holding the session file, its audio files, the bounces and a documentation PDF.
These are the five that cost marks every semester. None of them is about mixing ability. All five are avoidable in the twenty minutes before you present. 
Each mistake, the sound that gives it away, and what to do instead
The mistakeWhat you hearWhat to do instead
Running out of time before the second mix playsThe talk ends with an apology and a rushed thirty seconds of audio.Rehearse with a timer once. If you cannot get to the second mix by minute five, cut the setup, not the listening.
Playing the two mixes at different levelsThe louder one sounds better to everyone in the room, including you.Match loudness before you present. The point is the difference in decisions, not in gain.
Talking over the audioNobody can evaluate the mix and follow your sentence at the same time.Set up the listen, stay quiet through it, then explain.
Describing every change you madeTen minutes of small moves with no thread. The audience cannot tell which mattered.Pick three decisions. Say why each one was made and what it cost.
Files that will not open on the room machineA session that needs a plug-in the lab does not have, or a cloud link that will not load.Bring bounced WAVs on a drive. Treat the session as a bonus, not the plan.

Final Mix and Final Exam: Study Guide
[IMAGE: Professional Practice Bounce Specification]
Figure 1. Professional Practice Bounce Specification.
This guide covers the topic areas tested on the final exam. The exam draws 50 questions from a bank of 100+. Study every section - questions are pulled from all areas. 
[IMAGE: Note] 
Note: Questions are multiple choice with one correct answer. Focus on the "why" behind each concept, not just the name - many questions ask you to apply the concept to a real scenario. 
1. macOS Finder Fundamentals
You need to know keyboard shortcuts and how the macOS file system is organized. 
Essential Finder Keyboard Shortcuts
Shortcut
Action
Command+W
Close the active window
Command+N
Open a new Finder window
Command+Shift+N
Create a new folder
Command+Q
Quit the frontmost application
Command+Option+Esc
Force Quit dialog
Command+Shift+G
Go to Folder (type a path)
Command+Shift+Period
Show/hide hidden files
Command+Option+C
Copy file path as text
Command+C then Command+Option+V
Cut and paste (move) a file
User folder structure to know: 
~ - the tilde is shorthand for your Home folder (e.g., /Users/yourname/) 
~/Downloads - default location for downloaded files 
~/Library/Preferences - stores application preference files for the logged-in user 
The Users folder sits at the root of the startup volume, and each account has its own subfolder inside it 
2. Compression
Compression is one of the most-tested topics. Know every control and what it actually does to the audio. 
Compressor Controls
Control
What It Does
Threshold
The level at which compression begins. Signal above this gets reduced.
Ratio
How much reduction is applied. 4:1 means 4 dB over threshold yields only 1 dB output.
Attack
How fast the compressor reacts to a signal exceeding threshold. Fast attack clamps transients.
Release
How long gain reduction takes to stop after the signal falls below threshold.
Knee
Soft knee = gradual onset around threshold. Hard knee = abrupt onset exactly at threshold.
Makeup Gain
Boosts output to restore level lost from gain reduction.
Sidechain
Triggers compression from an external or filtered signal rather than the main input.
GR Meter
Gain Reduction - shows how many dB are being reduced in real time.
Key concept - parallel compression: Blend a heavily compressed version of a signal with the uncompressed original. The result retains transient energy while adding density and sustain. This is often called New York compression. 
Key concept - ratio at infinity:1 becomes a limiter - the output cannot exceed the threshold regardless of input level. 
3. Gates
Gates reduce or mute signals below a threshold. Know every control, especially hysteresis. 
Gate Controls
Control
What It Does
Threshold
Level below which the gate closes and reduces or silences the signal.
Hysteresis
A second, lower threshold the signal must drop below before the gate closes. Prevents chattering on borderline signals like snare rattle.
Attack
How fast the gate opens when the signal exceeds threshold.
Hold
How long the gate stays open after the signal drops below threshold, before the release phase begins.
Release
How fast the gate closes after the hold time expires.
Range
Maximum attenuation applied when closed. -80 dB = nearly silent; -20 dB = a noticeable but not complete cut.
[IMAGE: Warning] 
Hysteresis vs. threshold: The threshold is the level at which the gate opens. Hysteresis determines when it closes - specifically, it sets a second threshold below the main threshold that the signal must drop beneath before the gate shuts. This gap prevents the gate from rapidly flapping open and closed (chattering) on a signal that sits right around the threshold. 
4. Melodyne and ARA in Pro Tools
ARA stands for Audio Random Access. It is an extension standard that allows Melodyne to integrate directly into the Pro Tools timeline and access the full audio file non-destructively - no need to bounce or route audio outside the session. 
How to open Melodyne ARA in Pro Tools: Right-click the clip in the Edit window and choose Melodyne from the clip context menu (or use the Clip menu at the top). This is different from inserting Melodyne as a plugin on the track insert - the ARA workflow gives Melodyne full file access and timeline awareness. 
Melodyne Key Concepts
Term
Definition
Blob
A single detected note or pitch event displayed as an editable object in Melodyne.
Melodic algorithm
Best for monophonic sources such as lead vocals or single-note instruments.
Polyphonic algorithm
For complex material with multiple simultaneous pitches (chords, full mix).
Pitch Modulation tool
Adjusts the amount of vibrato or pitch variation within a single note.
Formant shift
Adjusts the resonant character of the sound independently from pitch. Prevents the chipmunk effect when transposing up.
Double-clicking a blob
Splits the blob into two separate editable note events.
5. Beat Mapping and Tempo in Pro Tools
Beat mapping aligns the Pro Tools tempo grid to a recorded performance that was played freely (not to a click). Once done, editing tools like Beat Detective and Elastic Audio can work in musical time. 
Identify Beat (Command+I): Place the cursor on a downbeat, press Command+I to tell Pro Tools that point is a beat. Repeat across the performance to define the tempo map. 
Beat Detective: Analyzes transients in a selection to generate bar and beat markers automatically. The Conform function trims and fills clips to align beats to the grid. 
Tempo ruler: Displays all tempo events in the session. Edit here to change tempo at specific points in the timeline. 
Elastic Audio must be enabled on a track before the track's audio will conform when the tempo grid changes. 
Bar|Beat Marker Generation in Beat Detective creates the actual tempo map entries from detected beats. 
Groove Template Extraction captures the timing feel of a performance so it can be applied to other tracks. 
6. Elastic Audio
Elastic Audio is Pro Tools' real-time time-stretching engine. Choose the right algorithm for your source material. 
Elastic Audio Algorithms
Algorithm
Best For
Key Characteristic
Polyphonic
Full mix, guitar chords, complex layered sources
Handles multiple simultaneous pitches
Rhythmic
Drums, percussion, loops with clear transients
Optimized for transient-heavy material
Monophonic
Lead vocals, single-note melodic instruments, spoken word
Changes duration while preserving pitch
Varispeed
Creative pitch-and-time effects
Changes pitch and timing together, like tape speed
X-Form
Highest quality time stretching for critical use
Offline/rendered only - no real-time processing
Other Elastic Audio terms to know: 
Warp marker: A reference point placed on a transient. Drag it to shift timing. Segments between warp markers stretch or compress independently. 
Analysis pass: Pro Tools scans the audio to detect and mark transient events before warping can occur. 
Rendered mode: Pre-calculates stretching and writes new audio files to disk, reducing CPU load during playback. 
TCE Trim tool: Drag a clip edge to stretch or compress the audio duration to fit the new boundary. 
Quantize to grid: Places warp markers on detected transients and stretches/compresses segments between them to align beats to the grid - it does not cut and move clips. 
7. Pro Tools Fundamentals
Pro Tools Terms and Functions
Term / Feature
Definition
Tab to Transients
When enabled, the Tab key jumps the cursor to the next detected transient in the audio.
Clip Gain handle
The thin line at the top of a clip. Drag to adjust gain for that clip only, independent of the track fader.
Playlist
A lane holding a sequence of clips on a track. Multiple playlists allow alternate takes on the same track.
Trim tool
Shortens or lengthens a clip's boundaries by dragging its edges.
Spot mode
Place a clip at an exact timecode or bar/beat location by entering a value in a dialog.
Memory Location
Saves named markers, selections, zoom settings, or other session states for instant recall.
Separate Clip (Command+E)
Splits the selected clip at the cursor or selection boundaries into two or more clips.
Bus
An internal routing path. Sends audio from multiple tracks to a single destination such as an aux track or output.
Pre-Fader send
The send level is tapped before the track fader. Moving the fader does not affect the send level.
Consolidate Clip
Renders a new continuous audio file from a clip or selection, including all edits and fades.
AudioSuite vs. AAX
AudioSuite processes offline and writes a new audio file. AAX plugins process in real time as inserts.
Loop Playback
Continuously repeats playback of the selected timeline region.
8. EQ
Q (bandwidth): Controls the width of the frequency range affected by a bell band. Narrow Q = surgical. Wide Q = broad color. 
High-pass filter (HPF): Passes frequencies above the cutoff, attenuates those below. Use on vocals and guitars to remove low-end rumble. 
Shelf vs. bell: A shelf affects all frequencies above or below a set point. A bell affects a band centered on a chosen frequency. 
Frequency masking: When two instruments share the same frequency range, one reduces the audibility of the other. EQ can carve space for each instrument. 
Subtractive EQ approach: Cut problem frequencies before boosting desirable ones. 
9. Reverb and Delay
Pre-delay: A short gap between the dry signal and reverb onset. Preserves clarity and definition of the source. Longer pre-delay pushes the reverb back in the mix. 
Decay time (RT60): How long the reverb tail takes to fall 60 dB after the source stops. 
Convolution vs. algorithmic reverb: Convolution uses an impulse response recording of a real space. Algorithmic uses mathematical models to simulate rooms. 
Feedback / regeneration: Controls the number of repeats in a delay. Higher feedback = more repeats before silence. 
Slapback delay: A single short delay (roughly 40-120 ms) with one repeat and no feedback. Common on rockabilly/country vocals and guitar. 
10. Signal Flow and Mixing
Gain staging: Setting appropriate levels at each stage (mic preamp, interface, DAW) to maximize signal-to-noise ratio and prevent clipping anywhere in the chain. 
Peak vs. RMS: Peak meters show instantaneous maximums. RMS shows averaged power, which correlates more closely to perceived loudness. 
Headroom: The distance between your operating level and 0 dBFS. Always leave headroom on the master bus before mastering. 
Aux track: Receives audio from bus inputs. Used for effects returns, sub-mix groups, and stem routing. 
Phase cancellation: When a close mic and room mic are combined, the time delay between them causes comb filtering. Inverting polarity on one mic can often correct this. 
Stem: A pre-mixed group of related tracks printed as a stereo file (e.g., all drums together as one file). 
Mono compatibility: A mix is mono compatible when summing L+R to a single channel does not cause significant cancellation or tonal change. 
11. Mid/Side (MS) Processing
Mid channel (M): The sum of left and right (L+R). Represents the center of the stereo image - kick, bass, lead vocal. 
Side channel (S): The difference (L-R). Represents spatial spread, room ambience, and wide-panned elements. 
Narrowing the image: Attenuate the Side channel. Boosting Side widens the image. 
MS mic setup: A forward-facing cardioid (M) combined with a sideways figure-8 (S). The two signals are decoded in post to produce a stereo pair. 
12. Audio Fundamentals
Nyquist theorem: Sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency to capture. At 44.1 kHz, the upper limit is 22.05 kHz. 
Bit depth: Determines dynamic range and noise floor. Each additional bit adds approximately 6 dB of dynamic range. 24-bit = roughly 144 dB theoretical range. 
Clipping: Occurs when a signal exceeds 0 dBFS. The waveform is truncated at the maximum value, producing harsh distortion. 
Transient: The sharp, short-duration peak at the attack of a sound. Kick drum beater impact, guitar pick attack, consonant sounds in speech. 
Dithering: Low-level noise added to mask quantization errors when reducing bit depth (e.g., 24-bit session exported to 16-bit for CD). Applied once, at the final export stage. 
Master bus limiter: Prevents the output from exceeding the ceiling (typically -0.1 or -0.3 dBFS) to avoid digital clipping on delivery. 
Latency vs. delay: Latency is unintended system lag. Delay is an intentional time-based effect. 
[IMAGE: Tip] 
Study tip: For each control (threshold, attack, release, Q, pre-delay, etc.), practice explaining it in one sentence starting with "This controls..." Then practice explaining the consequence of setting it too high or too low. That is the level of understanding the exam questions test.

Step-by-Step Workflow
Open the final session copy, confirm that all audio files are online, and save a dated version before making final changes. 
Listen from start to finish while checking edits, automation, routing, effects returns, and master-bus headroom. 
Make a precise bounce selection, use the required delivery format and sample rate, and import the bounce back into the session. 
Listen to the imported delivery in full and verify its file name, duration, start, end, and absence of clipping before uploading the required files.

ControlWhat it does

Sessions: Accessing Course Files on the Network Drive (DGM Assets)
[IMAGE: Flat diagram of connecting to a network share and locating the course folder]
Figure 1. Connecting to the share and finding the course assets. Three steps, and the path is the part worth writing down.
Assignment files for this course are stored on the UVU network. Follow the instructions below for your lab location. You must be connected to the UVU network or UVU Wi-Fi for this to work. 
Note: These instructions apply any time an assignment page tells you to find files in the DGM Assets folder. Bookmark the server address so you only have to do this once per computer. 
Mac Lab Computers
Use the Connect to Server dialog in Finder to mount the network drive. 
Step 1: Open Finder. Press Command + K on your keyboard. The Connect to Server dialog will open. 
Step 2: In the Server Address field at the top, type or paste the following path exactly: 
smb://af3.ad.uvu.edu/DGM Assets/Adam Olson/Core Mixing 
Step 3: Click Connect. If prompted, enter your UVU username and password. 
Step 4 (Optional but recommended): To save this address for future use, click the + button next to the server address field before clicking Connect. It will appear in your Favorite Servers list the next time you open Connect to Server. 
Step 5: The Core Mixing folder will mount on your Desktop and appear in the Finder sidebar under Locations. Open it and navigate to the folder named in your assignment instructions. 
Reference: The Connect to Server dialog should look like the screenshot posted with this page. The server address bar at the top is where you type the path. The + button to save favorites is at the bottom left of the dialog. 
Windows Lab Computers
On Windows, use File Explorer to connect to the network path. 
Step 1: Open File Explorer (Windows key + E). 
Step 2: Click in the address bar at the top of File Explorer (or press Ctrl + L to select it). Type the following path, replacing the forward slashes with backslashes and the leading smb: with nothing: 
\\af3.ad.uvu.edu\DGM Assets\Adam Olson\Core Mixing 
Step 3: Press Enter. If prompted for credentials, enter your UVU username and password. Your username format is typically uvu\yourusername. 
Step 4: The Core Mixing folder will open in File Explorer. Navigate to the folder named in your assignment instructions.

Sessions: Free DAW Session Track Downloads
[IMAGE: Flow from downloading a multitrack archive to an open session]
Figure 1. Download, expand, import, match the sample rate. The last step is the one that bites.
Use these sources to find multitrack recordings, stems, and full session files for mixing practice. Most are available as WAV stems you can import into Pro Tools, Logic Pro, Cubase, Nuendo, or any DAW. A few sites offer native session formats. Always read each site's licensing terms before using tracks in any public project. 
Note: These are external sites. File availability, formats, and licensing terms change over time. Verify licensing before distributing any mix made with these tracks. 
Featured Resource
Cambridge Music Technology - Mixing Secrets Free Multitrack Library 
The most extensive free multitrack library available. Hundreds of real commercial recordings across virtually every genre, provided by the original artists and engineers specifically for mixing practice. Tracks are pre-gain-staged and ready to load. This is the primary recommended source for this program. 
cambridge-mt.com - Mixing Secrets Free Multitrack Library 
Multitrack and Stem Libraries
Sounds to Sample - Free Multitracks 
A curated collection of free multitrack sessions including live drums, bass, guitars, and full band recordings. Sessions are available as individual WAV files organized by song. Good for pop, rock, and R&B mixing practice. 
soundstosample.com - Free Multitracks 
Produce Like A Pro - Free Multitracks 
Warren Huart's site regularly posts free multitrack sessions from professional recordings. Sessions span pop, rock, blues, and acoustic genres. Each download includes stems ready to import into any DAW. 
producelikeapro.com - Free Multitrack Downloads 
Mike Senior - Mixing Secrets Multitrack 
The companion site to the book Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio. Offers direct links to multitrack downloads organized by the chapters and techniques covered in the book. Useful if you are working through that text alongside coursework. 
cambridge-mt.com - Mixing Secrets Multitrack Resource Page 
Open License and Archive Sources
ccMixter 
A community music remix site where artists upload stems and a cappella tracks under Creative Commons licenses. Useful for finding vocal stems, instrument loops, and partial session components. Requires checking individual track licenses before use. 
ccmixter.org 
Free Music Archive - Multitracks 
The Free Music Archive hosts a smaller but curated selection of multitrack recordings available under open licenses. Search for "multitrack" or "stems" to filter relevant results. Most files are WAV or AIFF. 
freemusicarchive.org 
DAW-Specific Session Files
Avid - Pro Tools Demo Sessions and Sample Content 
Avid provides demo sessions and sample content through the Avid Resource Center. Content includes native Pro Tools sessions for mixing practice and software demonstration. Log in with an Avid account to access downloads. 
resources.avid.com - Avid Resource Center 
Steinberg - Cubase and Nuendo Demo Projects 
Steinberg distributes demo projects with Cubase and Nuendo installers and through their download portal. These are native .cpr session files that open directly in Cubase or Nuendo. Useful for exploring routing and plugin chains in a professionally structured session. 
steinberg.net - Cubase Demo Projects 
Apple - Logic Pro Demo Projects 
Apple ships a set of demo projects with Logic Pro, accessible from the Project Chooser under the Demo Projects category. These are native Logic sessions featuring professional productions across multiple genres. They require Logic Pro and do not export as cross-DAW stems without manual bouncing. 
support.apple.com - Open a Logic Pro Demo Project 
Drum and Instrument-Specific Multitracks
J3T Drum Tracks - Free Drum Multitracks 
J3T Drum Tracks publishes free multitrack drum sessions recorded with fifteen to sixteen microphones, from close mics on every drum out to vintage valve and ribbon room mics. Files are 24 bit, 44.1 kHz. Because every mic arrives on its own track, these are the closest thing to a real tracked drum session you can get without booking one, and they are ideal for phase alignment, overhead balance, room blending and parallel bus compression practice. 
j3tdrumtracks.com - Free Drum Stems 
Licensing reminder: Free download does not mean free for all uses. Many of these tracks are licensed for personal practice and education only. Do not distribute mixes publicly, submit to streaming platforms, or use in commercial work without reviewing the specific license for each track.
